area: Downtown Madison Isthmus, Madison, Wisconsin — the ~1.5-mile-wide neck of land between Lake Mendota (north) and Lake Monona (south), running from the UW-Madison campus edge at the southwest to the Williamson Street / Marquette district at the east, with the Wisconsin State Capitol on the high point in the middle.
biomes: Granite civic plateau (Capitol hill — the isthmus high point, formal, cold, echoing)
Pedestrian commercial canyon (State Street — 4-6 story masonry walls, no cars, buskers)
Campus threshold (Library Mall / 700-800 blocks — fountain, kiosks, student churn)
Mansion Hill Victorian garden district (brick, wrought iron, tiny hidden pocket greens)
Lake Mendota north shore park & beach (grass, sand, boathouse, sailboats)
Lake Monona south shore concrete terrace (curved white decks over water, wind, causeway)
Brick warehouse rail row (Williamson St — Romanesque brick, rusticated stone, turrets)
Arena / big-box civic bulk (Kohl Center superblock, cantilevered concrete)
Neoclassical government stone block (Municipal Building, colonnades, limestone)
Isthmus land bridge / shoreline causeway (John Nolen Drive, the narrows)

landmarks.name: Wisconsin State Capitol
landmarks.character: The single dominating structure of the isthmus and the map's obvious central spire. Beaux-Arts, built in five phases 1906-1917 by George B. Post & Sons, faced entirely in white Bethel granite from Vermont. Plan is a symmetrical cross/X: four equal wings radiating to the four corners of the square, each wing roughly 125 ft wide, 84 ft high and 187 ft long, so the building has four equal front doors and no back. Crowned by the only granite dome in the United States — the largest granite dome in the world — topped by Daniel Chester French's gilded bronze 'Wisconsin' statue, 15 ft 5 in tall and three tons. Total height 284 ft 5 in from ground floor to the top of the statue, about three feet shorter than the US Capitol. Interior is 43 kinds of stone from six countries and eight states: cold polished marble, brass rails, a rotunda under a 34-ft-diameter Edwin Blashfield dome mural (1912), mosaics by Kenyon Cox. Sound carries — footsteps and voices echo up the rotunda drum. An observation deck sits under the dome colonnade. A 1990 state law caps any structure within one mile of the Capitol center at 1,032.8 ft above sea level, so nothing in the whole downtown competes with it; every sightline in the isthmus terminates here. Address 2 E. Main St.
landmarks.game_idea: The final Gym / Elite Four tower and the region's League HQ. Four wings = four equal entrances, so the player can attack it from any of the four corners of the square — each wing is a different elemental sub-gym (Ground/Water/Fire/Electric) and you must clear all four before the rotunda unlocks. The rotunda is a vertical puzzle: the mural above is a map, and light through the drum rotates a floor mosaic to reveal a staircase. The Champion waits on the dome observation deck, in the open air, wind, with the whole isthmus visible below. The height-limit law becomes lore: 'no tower in the province may rise above the Dome' — a decree that explains why the whole map is low-rise, and a plot hook when someone breaks it.

landmarks.name: Capitol Square (Capitol Park and the Concourse)
landmarks.character: Nine and a half acres of landscaped grounds forming the square at the dead center of James Duane Doty's 1836 plat (surveyed with J. V. Suydam). A one-way ring road, the Concourse, wraps it; the four street faces are Mifflin, Pinckney, Main and Carroll, and the four corners open onto radiating avenues — State Street, Wisconsin Avenue, East and West Washington Avenue, King Street and Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard. Horace W. S. Cleveland was invited in 1872 to design the park with serpentine meandering walks and four fountains; the elaborate plan was never fully built, and what exists now is big shade trees, wide lawn panels, straight diagonal walks to the four corner entrances, benches, and a hard granite terrace at the base of the building. It is the region's default gathering ground: on Saturdays from April to November the Dane County Farmers' Market — the largest producer-only farmers' market in the country, roughly 150 vendors on the Square in summer out of a season pool of about 275 — completely encircles the Capitol, moving counterclockwise, shoulder to shoulder. Wednesday market moves to MLK Jr. Blvd. Concerts, Art Fair on the Square, protests, and the whole city's civic noise land here.
landmarks.game_idea: The hub town's central plaza and the rotating shop layer. The Square is a ring you walk around, and a day/week clock changes what is on it: on Market Day it becomes a full circular bazaar of ~150 stalls — berries, cheese, honey, seedlings, herbs — where the ONLY way to buy certain crafting reagents and rare berries is to walk the ring counterclockwise before the vendors pack up at noon. Walking against the crowd flow is a movement debuff, which teaches players the local etiquette. Off-market days the ring is empty lawn with trainers, a busker, and a couple of NPCs on benches. Four diagonal walks from the four corners feed into the Capitol Gym, so the Square doubles as the approach ramp to the endgame.

landmarks.name: State Street (whole corridor)
landmarks.character: The isthmus's spine and the map's main artery: 0.78 miles (1.26 km), eight blocks, running from the Capitol's southwest corner at Carroll and Mifflin west to Lake Street and Library Mall at the edge of UW-Madison. Dead-straight, gently rising and falling, walled on both sides by continuous 3-6 story brick and stone storefront blocks so it reads as a canyon. Converted starting June 1974 from a four-lane road into a transit/pedestrian mall for about $15 million: roadway narrowed to two lanes, sidewalks made extra wide, brick paving, planters, bollards. Only city buses, fire apparatus, police, bicycles, delivery vehicles and pedestrians. The 100-600 blocks are the transit mall; the 700 and 800 blocks are a full pedestrian mall with no through traffic at all. Roughly 150 businesses. The soundscape is buskers, jugglers, drummers, a hammered dulcimer, bus air brakes, and skateboards on brick. Rough patches are real — 31 businesses closed by summer 2020, about 75 were damaged in the 2020 unrest, and vacancies still cluster at the Capitol end.
landmarks.game_idea: The linear connecting Route between the hub town (Capitol Square) and the campus zone — a Route made of shops instead of grass. Eight blocks = eight discrete segments with their own encounter table and their own shopkeeper. Because buses still run it, a Bus mechanic gives fast travel between block gates once you've unlocked each one, but riding skips the encounters and the buskers, so speedrunners lose items. Street performers are mini-bosses that battle you with music-timing minigames; beat all of them along the length and you earn a 'Busker's Ear' ability.

landmarks.name: State Street 100-200 blocks (Capitol end)
landmarks.character: The formal, institutional head of the street, spilling directly out of the Capitol's west corner. Widest and grandest section, with the biggest buildings on the corridor: the Overture Center's glass-and-limestone wall on the 200 block's south side, MMoCA's angular glass prow at State and Henry, and the Orpheum Theatre's big vertical marquee sign. This is also the corridor's weakest retail stretch — the 100 block has carried large, long-running vacancies after several proposed redevelopments fell through, so you get monumental cultural facades next to papered-over storefronts. Feels grand, a little empty and echoing on weekdays; floods with people on show nights and market mornings.
landmarks.game_idea: The 'gateway plaza' segment — high-production-value architecture, low population. Use it as the tutorial-adjacent zone where the theater and museum NPCs live and where the vacancies are literal: boarded shopfronts you can enter as small, procedurally re-dressed dungeon rooms ('the Empty Storefronts'), each holding a squatting Pokemon nest that respawns. A side quest chain lets the player re-tenant the vacant units one by one, and each restored shop permanently adds a vendor to the map — turning urban blight into a visible base-building progression.

landmarks.name: State Street 300-400 blocks (middle)
landmarks.character: The transitional middle of the street where the scale drops and the building line gets fine-grained — narrow 20-to-30-foot storefronts, older brick, upper-floor apartments with window AC units and hanging plants. Retail here has thinned to a few holdouts (a shoe store, a clothing shop) and is now mostly food businesses and vacancies. Feels the most ordinary and lived-in stretch: takeout counters, a barber, stairwell doors to walk-up apartments, delivery bikes, side alleys and service doors mid-block. Cross streets (Gorham/Johnson on the north side, Dayton) feed in and out.
landmarks.game_idea: The everyday shop belt and the item-economy backbone: this is where the Poke Mart equivalents, the food vendors who sell healing consumables, and the Move Deleter/Name Rater live. Make it the segment with the most side-alley doors — a hidden back-alley network behind the 300-400 blocks that connects storefronts to each other, used as a stealth/shortcut layer and as the home of a mildly shady item broker. Anything you can't buy on the street, you can buy behind it.

landmarks.name: State Street 500-600 blocks (student commercial core)
landmarks.character: The loudest, densest, youngest stretch — squarely student-facing. The 500 block is fast-casual chains stacked side by side (fried chicken, burgers, sandwiches, burritos, tacos) plus a big coffee house, interleaved with genuine Madison holdouts like a basement record store. The 600 block is the corridor's most striking old/new collision: mom-and-pop storefronts directly abutting a big-box store, with an underground speakeasy-style cocktail bar operating since 1998 next door. Bright signage, neon, queues out doors at 1 a.m., pizza-by-the-slice smell, bikes chained to every rack. Highest foot traffic on the whole street.
landmarks.game_idea: The bustling market district and the natural Pokemon Center / restaurant-buff zone. Every food vendor sells a temporary stat-buff meal, and the buffs stack badly on purpose, so overeating before a battle is a real (funny) mistake. Put a hidden basement dungeon under the 600 block reached through the record shop and the speakeasy — a two-entrance underground level, dark, low-ceilinged, full of Sound- and Dark-type encounters, where a DJ-themed trainer battles you over a beat. The above/below contrast (chain-store brightness vs. subterranean speakeasy) is the whole design hook.

landmarks.name: State Street 700-800 blocks and Library Mall (campus end)
landmarks.character: The pedestrian mall proper — no buses, no cars, brick and concrete paving edge to edge, widening from a street into a plaza. The 700 block is typically lined with food carts and craft vendors. It opens into Library Mall, an open paved square with a fountain, benches, big trees, and a low horizon compared to the canyon behind you. Ringed by campus institutions: Memorial Library, the University Club, the Wisconsin Historical Society building, and the University Book Store. This is where downtown stops being commercial and becomes academic — the crowd shifts to backpacks, bikes, flyer tables, chalked sidewalks, protests, and preachers on upturned crates.
landmarks.game_idea: The campus gate and the Route's terminus town square. Library Mall is the natural Pokemon Center + PC + tutor cluster, and the fountain is a fixed Water-type encounter/fishing spot dropped implausibly in the middle of a plaza. Memorial Library becomes the region's Move Tutor / lore archive dungeon: stacks that go down, not up, with a card-catalog puzzle that grants TMs. The food carts on the 700 block are a rotating daily vendor list — different carts on different in-game days — giving a soft reason to return.

landmarks.name: Museum Mile
landmarks.character: Not an official designation — a descriptive name for the roughly one-mile walk of museums running from Capitol Square down State Street to the campus. The chain: the Wisconsin Veterans Museum at 30 W. Mifflin on the Square (a Smithsonian Affiliate since 2014, two galleries covering the Civil War to the present, with a large Battle of Antietam diorama and three full-scale aircraft — a Sopwith Camel, a P-51 Mustang, and a Huey — hung in the space); the Wisconsin Historical Museum at 30 N. Carroll (a converted former hardware store opened 1986, now gone — last exhibits closed Nov 2022, demolished Oct 2023, being replaced by the $112.3 million Wisconsin History Center, groundbreaking April 2025, expected 2028); the Madison Children's Museum at 100 N. Hamilton (a five-story former office building bought in 2005, opened Aug 2010, LEED Gold, with an accessible green roof); MMoCA at 227 State; Overture's four visual art galleries; and, at the far campus end, the Chazen Museum of Art. Coordinate given is the Veterans Museum, one anchor of a corridor, not the corridor's center. Feels like a strung-out chain rather than a district — you walk past ordinary storefronts between institutions.
landmarks.game_idea: A collection quest spine, not a single location: the Museum Mile is the region's Pokedex-completion mechanic made physical. Each museum is a small optional dungeon holding one Fossil/Relic, and turning in a Relic to the right curator revives a prehistoric Pokemon or unlocks a lore entry. Build in a genuinely great beat: the Historical Museum is a construction site — a hole in the ground behind fencing — for most of the game, and completing a late-game questline finishes the new History Center, which opens as a fully new interior with all the region's lore in one place. A museum that gets built while you play is worth the whole gimmick.

landmarks.name: Overture Center for the Arts
landmarks.character: Occupies a whole State Street block at 201 State, built with $205 million in philanthropic gifts from Jerome Frautschi and Pleasant Rowland and designed by César Pelli; opened Sept 19, 2004, replacing the old Madison Civic Center while swallowing and restoring the 1928 Capitol Theater inside it. Long limestone-and-glass street wall with a tall curved-glass entry; inside, a very large light-filled atrium spine runs the depth of the block and is used as public living room and gallery. Multiple stacked halls: Overture Hall (2,255 seats, with a custom-built pipe organ), Capitol Theater (1,089), the Playhouse (347), Promenade Hall (252), the Rotunda Stage (350), plus studios and four visual art galleries and the adjoining Madison Museum of Contemporary Art. Feel: hushed, bright, generous, slightly overscaled for its street — a cathedral of a lobby that is free to walk through.
landmarks.game_idea: The Sound/Performance Gym, and a vertical multi-stage dungeon. Five venues of descending size = five nested challenge tiers; you fight your way from the tiny Playhouse up to Overture Hall, where the Gym Leader is a conductor whose Pokemon attack on the beat of the pipe organ and the player must time inputs to the score. The organ itself is the puzzle: pulling the right stops opens passages between halls. The atrium is a free rest/social hub with no battles at all — a deliberate safe room in the middle of a dungeon, which makes the halls feel more dangerous by contrast.

landmarks.name: Monona Terrace Community and Convention Center
landmarks.character: Frank Lloyd Wright's 1938 civic-center dream, finally built after his death: approved by referendum in 1992, construction began Jan 25, 1995, opened July 18, 1997 — nearly 60 years after the design. Exterior is Wright's; interiors by former Wright apprentice Anthony Puttnam of Taliesin Architects. Wright spent some 63,000 hours of studio time on it over 21 years for $250 in fees. 250,000 sq ft of steel and concrete, all curves and circles: white arcs, drums, circular motifs, sweeping ramps, banded parapets. Built out over John Nolen Drive on the Lake Monona shore, with a 68,000-square-foot rooftop garden (the William T. Evjue Rooftop Gardens) whose pedestrian plaza extends about 90 feet out over the lake. It contains an exhibition hall, ballroom, banquet hall and media center. It reads as a white terrace stitching the Capitol's civic axis down to the water — the roof lines up back to Olin Terrace and the Capitol; from the roof you see the dome behind you and open lake ahead. Feel on the roof: exposed, windy, glaring white in sun, water on three sides.
landmarks.game_idea: The lakeside Water Gym and the region's port/ferry hub. The rooftop garden is the outdoor arena — a white circular battlefield cantilevered 90 feet over the water where knockbacks can genuinely send a Pokemon off the edge into the lake, forcing a Water-type or a recall. Below deck, the exhibition hall is a shifting convention floor whose layout changes with an in-game event calendar (one week a bug expo, one week a trade show), so the interior is never the same dungeon twice. Lore hook: a building designed by a master who died before it was built, raised 60 years later — perfect for a ruined-blueprint / ghost-architect side quest where you find the original 1938 drawings and discover what was left out.

landmarks.name: Machinery Row
landmarks.character: A long Romanesque Revival brick commercial block filling a full city block at 601-627 Williamson Street, about half a mile east of the Capitol at the Williamson/John Nolen corner. Built in stages roughly 1898-1912 (some sources to 1914) by Frank and Frederick Brown, designed by Allan Conover and Lew F. Porter. Rusticated sandstone base, white brick walls trimmed in Abelman stone and tile, round-arched window tops on the second story, corbelled brick cornice. A round tower with battlements crowns the northwest corner; a smaller turret with a conical roof caps the far end — so the block has a castle silhouette at both ends. Built to house agricultural-implement distributors who needed access to the east-side rail depots, hence 'Machinery.' Listed on the National Register April 12, 1982. Adaptively reused since: a long-running bicycle shop at 601, creative-professional office tenants, exposed stone walls, heavy timber beam ceilings, tall windows with Lake Monona views. Repeated large redevelopment schemes for the area have stalled.
landmarks.game_idea: The Steel-type Gym housed in an old machine works — the most obviously game-shaped building on the isthmus, because it already has two towers. Enter under the battlemented corner tower; the interior is a working dungeon of belt drives, line shafts, and conveyor puzzles left from the implement dealers, where you ride moving platforms and reroute power between floors. The bike shop stays canon: this is where you get the Bicycle, which is the classic gating item, so players must clear or at least visit the Row to unlock overworld speed. The conical turret at the far end is the Leader's office, all timber beams and lake windows.

landmarks.name: James Madison Park
landmarks.character: 12.63 acres of Lake Mendota waterfront at 614 E. Gorham St., a long green shelf between the street and the water on the isthmus's north shore — the biggest open green in the downtown. Open grassy panels used for pickup soccer and frisbee, a sand beach with no lifeguards and no swim ropes (water quality monitored Memorial Day to Labor Day), two full basketball courts, a sand volleyball court, two playgrounds, restrooms, a reservable picnic shelter, fishing access, and a canoe/kayak launch with storage racks. Two National Register buildings sit in and beside it: the 1915 Bernard-Hoover Boathouse on the shoreline, and the Gates of Heaven Synagogue at 302 E. Gorham — an 1863 building, the eighth-oldest surviving synagogue building in the United States, moved into the park and now a popular wedding venue for all faiths. Feel: sailboats and windsurfers offshore, geese, cottonwoods, a low seawall, sunset light off the water, and the noise of downtown dropping away behind you.
landmarks.game_idea: The waterfront route and the region's starter/surf zone — the first place the player touches Lake Mendota, so it's where Surf and the fishing rods pay off, with the boat launch as the departure point for lake routes and islands. The Gates of Heaven building is the quiet emotional beat: a tiny relocated 1863 sanctuary used as a shrine where players can bless, rename, or heal a Pokemon, with a caretaker NPC who has been there longer than the town. The boathouse is a small three-room dungeon with a Water/Ghost resident. Beach volleyball and basketball courts become optional minigame trainers with unique rewards.

landmarks.name: Period Garden Park
landmarks.character: A little over 10,000 square feet — about a quarter acre — at 110 E. Gorham St. at North Pinckney, in the Mansion Hill historic district. Among the very smallest parks in the city, and constantly mistaken by passersby for somebody's private front yard, because it literally was one: it sits on the parceled-off front lawn of the historic Keyes House at 102 E. Gorham, split off around 1973. Saved from redevelopment by neighborhood activists and dedicated May 8, 1977 by the Board of Park Commissioners and the Madison Landmarks Commission. Designed to recreate a Victorian-era garden of the sort common in this neighborhood in the 19th century: brick walkways, carved sandstone steps, layered perennial beds, a wrought-iron fence, deep shade. Enclosed, hushed, and completely invisible until you're standing at its gate — one block off a busy street and utterly still.
landmarks.game_idea: The secret garden — a hidden Grass/Fairy sanctuary the player can walk past a dozen times without noticing, entered through a gate that only appears once an NPC mentions it. Inside is a single-screen enclosed space with a Victorian planting scheme where a rare Fairy-type only appears in specific seasons and only if the player has done nothing loud beforehand (no battles that day). Make it the region's berry-cultivation and breeding node: the beds are plots, and the Keyes House caretaker is the gardener who teaches you to grow. Its size is the point — the smallest location on the map holding the rarest thing, rewarding players who explore laterally instead of forward.

landmarks.name: Kohl Center
landmarks.character: The bulk anchor of the isthmus's southwest end, at 601 W. Dayton St. at N. Frances, on the campus edge. Opened Jan 17, 1998, cost $76.4 million, designed by Venture Architects with HOK Sport and Heinlein Schrock Stearns; roughly 387,000 sq ft (some sources cite a larger total). Capacity 17,287 for basketball, 15,359 for hockey — by far the largest interior volume downtown. Built with cantilevered balconies rather than a setback bowl, modeled somewhat on the older Wisconsin Field House, so the upper decks hang steeply over the floor and the crowd feels stacked directly on top of the action. Dale Chihuly's blown-glass 'Mendota Wall' fills the front entrance in blues and greens. Includes the Nicholas-Johnson Pavilion and Plaza for practice space. Feel: a windowless brick-and-concrete mass on the street, and inside a dark bowl with a bright floor, deafening on game nights and cavernous and echoing when empty.
landmarks.game_idea: The Battle Tower / Colosseum — the postgame endless-challenge venue, and the only place with a real crowd. Cantilevered decks mean the audience is physically overhead, so crowd reaction becomes a mechanic: consecutive wins raise the crowd meter, which buffs your Pokemon's Attack and debuffs the opponent's accuracy, and a bad loss silences the building. The Chihuly glass wall in the lobby is a Water/Ice puzzle gate that lights up one glass form per streak milestone, giving players a visible trophy case built into the architecture. Ice-rink and hardwood configurations swap the arena's terrain type between visits.

landmarks.name: Madison Municipal Building
landmarks.character: A three-story Neoclassical Revival block at 215 Martin Luther King Jr. Blvd, one block off the Capitol on the Monona side, built 1927-1929 to designs from the U.S. Treasury Department under Acting Supervising Architect James A. Wetmore. U-shaped footprint on about two acres; steel-reinforced brick faced in limestone; a two-story Ionic colonnade across the front facade, a central entrance with three doorways under carved stone moldings, and a cornice and parapet at the roof. Served as Madison's main post office until 1979 and as the federal courthouse until the courts moved out; the city took it over and renamed it in 1980. Renovated 2016-2018 for $30.2 million: false ceilings pulled out, bricked-up original factory windows reopened, black paint stripped off fixtures, the original entrance hall restored, and modern systems threaded through 90-year-old bones. Feel: heavy, symmetrical, cool stone, a long formal lobby, and light now pouring through windows that were sealed for decades.
landmarks.game_idea: The region's administrative hub — the place with all the paperwork, which is funnier and more useful than another dungeon. Trainer registration, license renewals, permits (fishing, surfing, digging), the lost-and-found, and the office that stamps the forms letting you access restricted areas. The old post office identity makes it the mail and trade depot: a physical Pokemon delivery service where players send items and Pokemon to other trainers and receive packages. Hidden layer: the sealed-then-reopened windows and abandoned courtroom become a small optional dungeon on the top floor, where a Ghost-type has lived in the dark since the false ceilings went in — a monster that was literally created by a bad 1970s renovation.

landmarks.name: Central Library and the vanished Carnegie library
landmarks.character: Two buildings, one story. Madison's first purpose-built library opened Feb 23, 1906 at 206 N. Carroll St., funded by a $75,000 Carnegie grant, and housed the Library School of the Wisconsin Free Library Commission on its second floor; after the replacement opened it was demolished to make a parking lot. Its successor, built 1965 at 201 W. Mifflin St. and named the Bernard Schwab Library in 1990 for the director who shaped it, was a 95,000 sq ft mid-century civic box with an open, undercut street-level entry. In 2012-2013 MSR Design (architect Traci Lesneski) gutted and reinvented it rather than replacing it: a 25,000 sq ft expansion enclosed the formerly open entry in a glass atrium, added a partial third floor, cut light wells down through the slab, and put a rooftop terrace with a solar-equipped green roof on top; gallery space and a media commons went in. It reopened Sept 21, 2013 and reads as a new building wearing a 1965 building's skeleton — bright, vertical light shafts, exposed structure, art on the walls, and a genuinely public, well-used room in the middle of downtown.
landmarks.game_idea: The Archive / lore dungeon and a two-timeline puzzle. The current library is the safe, bright surface layer: research desks, the region's Pokedex database, and a Move Tutor in the media commons. But the light wells cut through the 1965 structure are the way down — descend into the retained mid-century bones beneath the 2013 skin, a dim, low-ceilinged concrete stack level of forgotten collections. The real payoff is the Carnegie building: it exists only as a parking lot on N. Carroll, and a late-game item lets the player see and enter its 1906 ghost — a full second library overlaid on an empty lot, with the old Library School still in session upstairs. One location, three eras, and the deepest one is a building the town paved over.

notes:
SOURCING AND CONFIDENCE. Coordinates marked "verified" came from OpenStreetMap Nominatim lookups or Wikipedia infoboxes for that specific named feature. Coordinates marked "rough" are honest approximations: for the State Street block-group entries I anchored each on a real OSM-geocoded street address inside that range (150, 350/450, 600 State St), so the point is real but stands for a multi-block stretch; the State Street corridor point is Wikipedia's single point for a 0.78-mile street; the Museum Mile point is the Wisconsin Veterans Museum, one anchor of a corridor with no true center. Nothing here was invented.

TWO AMBIGUITIES RESOLVED. (1) "Museum Mile" is not an official Madison designation — repeated searches surfaced only the unrelated Milwaukee Museum Mile. I treated it as a descriptive corridor of downtown museums from Capitol Square to campus, which is how it functions, and listed the actual member institutions. (2) "The old Central Library" is genuinely two things — the demolished 1906 Carnegie building at 206 N. Carroll and the 1965 Schwab building at 201 W. Mifflin that survives inside the 2013 renovation — so I covered both in one entry and built the game idea on the pair.

LIVE STATE OF THE MAP (as of 2026). The Wisconsin Historical Museum at 30 N. Carroll is currently a construction site: exhibits closed Nov 2022, demolition Oct 2023, groundbreaking April 2025 for the $112.3M Wisconsin History Center, expected to open around 2028 (one source says a new space "at the top of State Street" in 2027). If the map is meant to feel current, that block should be fenced hoarding, not a museum. State Street's 100 block also carries long-standing vacancies, and the pedestrian-mall extent has been shifting year to year (100-600 as transit mall since the 1970s, 700-800 fully pedestrian, with 400-600 trialed as full pedestrian mall in 2024 and scaled back for 2025).

MAP GEOMETRY WORTH EXPLOITING. The isthmus is a natural game map because it is a corridor with hard water edges on both sides and one dominant vertical landmark in the middle — a level designer would have to invent this. Three structural gifts: (a) the 1990 height-limit law capping everything within a mile of the Capitol at 1,032.8 ft above sea level means the dome is visible from nearly every location, so it works as a permanent wayfinding beacon and as a lore decree; (b) the Capitol's four-wing cross plan gives four equal approaches and six radiating avenues from the corners, so the hub has natural spoke routes rather than one entrance; (c) the two lakes let the north shore (James Madison Park, beach, boathouse, soft and green) and the south shore (Monona Terrace, John Nolen Drive, hard white concrete over water) read as completely different biomes despite being ten minutes apart.

SUGGESTED PROGRESSION SPINE. Campus end (Library Mall / Kohl Center) → east up State Street through the block segments → Capitol Square hub → out to the shores (James Madison Park north, Monona Terrace south) → east along Williamson to Machinery Row → back to the Capitol for the endgame. That is a single loop with the final gym at the center, which is unusual and better than a linear chain.

DENSITY NOTE FOR THE DESIGNER. The scale contrast is extreme and should be preserved rather than normalized: Period Garden Park is ~10,000 sq ft and Kohl Center is ~387,000 sq ft, and they are under a mile apart. Putting the rarest encounter in the smallest space (Period Garden Park) and the most repeatable content in the largest (Kohl Center) inverts the usual expectation in a way players notice.

area: University of Wisconsin–Madison campus and the Lake Mendota lakeshore, Madison, Dane County, Wisconsin, USA — a ~936-acre contiguous campus running roughly 3 miles WNW from State Street/Library Mall to Eagle Heights, wrapped along ~4 miles of Lake Mendota's south shore.
biomes: Glacial drumlin ridge (Bascom–Observatory spine): steep mown lawn, elm/oak allées, sandstone-and-limestone institutional buildings, 100 ft of relief in under 900 ft of run
Dense urban campus core / street-mall: Library Mall, State Street terminus, fountain plaza, brick pavers, food carts, Brutalist + contemporary museum blocks
Lakefront terrace + hardened shoreline: Memorial Union Terrace flagstone, seawalls, piers, sailboats, Alumni Park lawn — the one place the built campus touches open water directly
Lakeshore path corridor: narrow flat gravel/asphalt ribbon at lake level, willows, cottonwoods, boat racks, squeezed between water and bluff
Southern hardwood forest / oak savanna remnant: Muir Woods, Bill's Woods, Second Point Woods, Eagle Heights Woods — closed oak-hickory canopy, spring ephemerals, steep north-facing slopes
Restored tallgrass prairie: Biocore Prairie and Frautschi Point openings on old farm fields
Freshwater marsh and cattail wetland: Class of 1918 Marsh, University Bay Marsh, Triangle Marsh — northern pike nursery, dabbling ducks
Sandbar / delta / shallow bay: University Bay, the Willow Creek delta, the wave-built sandbar the Lakeshore Path rides on, and a second sandbar forming offshore
Channelized urban creek: Willow Creek, straightened, culverted, draining west Madison from as far out as Whitney Way
Open deep lake: Lake Mendota, 9,740 acres, 83 ft max depth, ice-covered most winters
Wooded lake bluff: Frautschi Point to Raymer's Cove to Eagle Heights — up to a 150 ft bluff face with slump, sand cove beaches, and long water views
Athletic/stadium district: Camp Randall bowl, the Field House, Kohl Center, flat former Civil War drill ground
Engineering/technical quarter: Engineering Mall, lab blocks, wind tunnels, machine shops, a 395,000 sq ft new build under construction
Agricultural research landscape: Babcock Hall dairy plant, Allen Centennial Garden, Linden Drive's ag-college axis — a working farm campus embedded in a city
Sacred earthwork ground: four surviving Late Woodland effigy mound groups (Observatory Hill, Willow Drive, Picnic Point, Eagle Heights), 650–1200 CE

landmarks.name: Bascom Hill
landmarks.character: The signature relief feature of the whole map and the reason the campus reads as vertical. A glacial drumlin lobe, deposited ~12,000 years ago; the Lakeshore Nature Preserve is explicit that Bascom Hill and Observatory Hill are not two hills but two parts of one drumlin. The classic climb runs 850 ft from the Park Street sidewalk up to the Lincoln statue, gaining 86 ft — about a 10 percent grade, 5.8 degrees. Crest sits at roughly 950 ft; Library Mall at its foot is ~861 ft; Lake Mendota is 850 ft. So the hill is a 100 ft wall between the flat downtown edge and everything west. The quad is lined with North Hall (1851, first university building, National Historic Landmark), South Hall (1855), Music Hall (1879, Gothic clock tower), and Science Hall (1885–88, second steel-framed building in the US, NHL 1994). NRHP Bascom Hill Historic District since 1974, called the most historic cluster of institutional buildings in Wisconsin. In winter students sled it on cafeteria trays; every spring it sprouts protest flags planted in the lawn.
landmarks.game_idea: THE ASCENT — a mandatory uphill route with a stamina/slip mechanic: in winter the slope is glazed and you slide back down unless you have the right badge item (Traction Boots). Trainers are staged in tiers up the slope so the fight gets harder with altitude, and the Lincoln statue at the top is a save/heal point that only activates once you've beaten every tier below it. Rock- and Ground-types dominate (it's a drumlin — the encounter flavor text calls out sand and gravel dumped by a glacier).

landmarks.name: Bascom Hall
landmarks.character: The administration building crowning the hill, begun 1857–59 as University Hall in Italian Renaissance Revival by William Tinsley, renamed for president John Bascom in 1920. Its dome burned off on October 10, 1916 and was never rebuilt — the flat, decapitated roofline is the point. Jeffersonian portico added 1894. Seated bronze Lincoln (1909) out front, a copy of Adolph Weinman's Hodgenville statue, whose lap students rub for luck and whose plinth carries the 'sifting and winnowing' free-speech plaque nearby.
landmarks.game_idea: THE DOMELESS GYM — the region's authority gym, at the literal high point of the human map. The Leader fights you in the roofless top-floor chamber where the dome used to be, open to sky and weather (rain/snow/sun from the overworld carries into the battle and changes move power). Beat them and the Lincoln statue outside stands up as a post-game secret boss, a Steel/Rock Colossus. The gym badge is shaped like a burned-off dome.

landmarks.name: Memorial Union and the Terrace
landmarks.character: Where the built campus touches open water with nothing in between. Opened October 5, 1928 (Arthur Peabody, Neo-Renaissance; 1939 Streamline Moderne theater wing), NRHP 2015. The Terrace, laid out from 1928 by Charlotte Peabody, is flagstone stepping down to the Lake Mendota seawall at ~869 ft, ten feet above lake level. About 2,000 sunburst chairs in John Deere green and Allis-Chalmers orange and yellow — farm-equipment colors, for the seasons — put out in spring and stacked away in fall, with a newer 'Mendota Blue' set added. Der Rathskeller inside is a German beer hall with painted murals. The Hoofers club (founded 1931) runs sailing, and the piers launch dinghies and paddleboards straight off the patio. In February the same water is a walkable ice sheet.
landmarks.game_idea: THE TERRACE — the region's social hub and Poké Center analogue, where NPC trainers idle in colored chairs and rotate seasonally: the chair set (and therefore who is sitting out here, and which Water/Ice encounters spawn off the pier) changes with the in-game season. Sign on with Hoofers to unlock Surf-by-sailboat across Lake Mendota, opening the whole north shore. In winter the same tiles freeze into an ice-puzzle floor and Water spawns are replaced by Ice.

landmarks.name: Library Mall
landmarks.character: The flat brick apron at the bottom of the hill, ~861 ft, hinging State Street (running a mile straight to the State Capitol) into the campus. Bounded by Memorial Library, the Wisconsin Historical Society, and Langdon Street. Hagenah Fountain (1958) at its center, inscribed 'Teachers and books are the springs from which flow the waters of knowledge' — it sat dry for six years before being restarted, and a ~$6M redesign would swap it for interactive sprays. Food carts, buskers, pamphleteers, the Class of 1932 flagpole. Described by the university as one of the most archaeologically rich campuses in the US, with 12,000 years of occupation under the pavers.
landmarks.game_idea: THE MALL MARKET — the starting-town plaza: food carts as vendor NPCs, a bulletin board issuing daily side-quests, and a fountain that only runs once you complete the 'restart the fountain' quest, after which it becomes a Water-type spawn puddle and a Fire-type weakness zone in the mall's evening battles. Digging minigame under the pavers surfaces Fossil items keyed to the site's deep occupation.

landmarks.name: Chazen Museum of Art
landmarks.character: Two-building museum on University Avenue, ~867 ft. Founded September 11, 1970 as the Elvehjem Museum in a Brutalist concrete box by Harry Weese, holding 1,600 works; the Machado-Silvetti addition opened October 2011 and roughly doubled it. The two halves are stitched together by a dramatic elevated bridge gallery. Collection now ~25,000 works. Free admission — no ticket desk, you just walk in.
landmarks.game_idea: THE BRIDGE GALLERY — a free-entry puzzle dungeon in two wings of totally different geometry (heavy Brutalist maze downstairs, bright glass volume upstairs) joined by a single elevated span. Ghost- and Psychic-types haunt the collection at night; the puzzle is matching paintings to the Pokémon that stepped out of them. The bridge is a one-way crossing until you find the counterweight switch, so the wings must be cleared in order.

landmarks.name: Babcock Hall and the Babcock Dairy Store
landmarks.character: A working dairy plant inside a research university, built 1951 on Linden Drive at ~871 ft, with a retail store attached. Named for Stephen Moulton Babcock, whose 1890 butterfat test let creameries pay farmers by quality and effectively made Wisconsin America's Dairyland by 1920; he and Harry Russell also developed cold-curing for cheese in 1897. The plant bottles milk, makes award-winning cheese, and produces the ice cream that has drawn queues out the door for 75+ years. Glass viewing windows let you watch the production floor.
landmarks.game_idea: THE CREAMERY — a berry/consumable crafting hub. Bring milk collected from Miltank-analogue encounters on the ag campus and the plant churns it into stat-boosting ice cream flavors; the butterfat-test machine downstairs is a grading minigame that determines how strong your batch is. Rare flavor-of-the-month recipes rotate on real in-game months. Ice/Fairy-type NPC specialist runs the counter.

landmarks.name: Camp Randall Stadium
landmarks.character: A 76,057-seat bowl on flat ground at ~866–880 ft, the oldest stadium in the Big Ten. The site was Camp Randall, a Union Army training camp in the Civil War named for Governor Alexander Randall; veterans blocked its conversion to building lots and the state bought it for the university in 1893. Stadium opened 1917 with 7,500 concrete seats. Between the third and fourth quarters the entire crowd does 'Jump Around' and the structure visibly and measurably shakes. The 1930 Field House sits alongside.
landmarks.game_idea: THE BOWL — a Battle Colosseum with tiered ranked ladders and a stadium-wide crowd meter. Every fourth turn of a boss fight the stands trigger JUMP AROUND: the arena floor shakes, Ground-type moves get a power spike, and non-grounded (Flying/Levitate) Pokémon are immune, so team composition has to plan around it. The Civil War camp history unlocks a Ghost-type night event on the drill ground.

landmarks.name: Union South
landmarks.character: The west-campus counterpart to Memorial Union, rebuilt and reopened April 15, 2011 — a $94.8M, 187,000 sq ft building, the university's first LEED Gold project, at ~873 ft. Contains The Sett, a three-story entertainment floor with a 30-foot climbing wall over recycled-rubber flooring, bowling lanes, billiards, and a live music stage, plus Varsity Hall and a hotel. Where Memorial Union is lakefront and 1928, this is inland, glassy, and loud.
landmarks.game_idea: THE SETT — a vertical indoor gauntlet. The 30-foot climbing wall is a timed ascent minigame gating a rooftop rival battle; bowling lanes host a Rolling/Ground-type accuracy minigame; the live stage runs a rhythm-battle mode where Sound-based moves crit on beat. Its LEED Gold credentials make it the region's solar/eco hub — the one place you can recharge Electric-type gear from the building's own systems.

landmarks.name: Engineering campus (Engineering Mall and Engineering Drive)
landmarks.character: The technical quarter on the south-west shoulder, ~875 ft: Engineering Hall at 1415 Engineering Drive, the Engineering Research Building at 1500, the Mechanical Engineering building at 1513 University Ave, Wendt Commons library. Engineering Mall is the green spine through it. Actively under demolition and construction — 1410 Engineering Drive, one of the oldest buildings here, is coming down for a $419 million, 395,000 sq ft new engineering center. Test cells, wind tunnels, and machine shops behind the facades; the district hums.
landmarks.game_idea: THE WORKS — an active construction site that physically changes between chapters: fenced hoardings, cranes, and a half-built tower that opens new floors as the story advances, so the same dungeon has to be re-entered later. Steel and Electric encounters; a wind-tunnel room where Flying-types get boosted and everything else has reduced accuracy. A researcher NPC upgrades your gear (bike, rod, detector) in exchange for scrap salvaged from 1410's demolition.

landmarks.name: Allen Centennial Garden
landmarks.character: A 2.5-acre free public botanical garden on Linden Drive at ~875 ft, wrapped around the Victorian Gothic Agricultural Dean's Residence of 1896 (architects Allan Conover and Lew Porter), built to keep the first ag dean, William Henry, from leaving. Broke ground 1985 on a gift from Ethel and Oscar Allen, opened 1989 for the Horticulture department's centennial. Roughly 14 named garden areas across ~27 distinct spaces — English cottage, iris meadow, Japanese garden, Wisconsin woodland, rock garden — each a different microclimate in a very small footprint.
landmarks.game_idea: GARDEN OF FOURTEEN ROOMS — a compact biome sampler where each walled garden room has its own encounter table and weather, so a two-minute walk cycles you through cottage, Japanese, woodland and rock habitats. Grass- and Bug-type breeding ground; the Dean's House is a Fairy/Ghost manor with a horticulturist NPC who cross-breeds your berries. Ideal early-game spot to fill dex entries you'd otherwise have to cross the region for.

landmarks.name: Lakeshore Nature Preserve
landmarks.character: 300 acres along 4 miles of Lake Mendota's south shore, held by the university as protected land and stitched together from 14+ named units: Muir Woods, Willow Creek Woods, Willow Beach, Triangle Marsh, University Bay Marsh, Class of 1918 Marsh, Picnic Point, Bill's Woods, Big Woods, Caretaker's Woods, Second Point Woods, Frautschi Point, Tent Colony Woods, Wally Bauman Woods, Eagle Heights Woods. Spine is the Lakeshore Path — the Howard Temin Path in the east, the Lake Mendota Path in the west. Open 4am–10pm. Four effigy mound groups sit inside it. The functional effect on the map: half of a Big Ten campus is wilderness, and you can walk from a lecture hall into oak forest in five minutes.
landmarks.game_idea: THE PRESERVE — a single large open-world wilderness zone (Safari Zone analogue) with sub-habitats rather than one flat encounter table, entered through gated trailheads that close at 10pm and reopen at 4am. Night entry requires a Ranger permit obtained late-game. A field-notebook mechanic: log species per named woodland and the preserve's ecologist NPC rewards completion per unit, not per zone, so thoroughness beats grinding.

landmarks.name: Picnic Point
landmarks.character: A nearly mile-long wooded peninsula reaching NE into Lake Mendota, tapering to a tip barely 6 ft above lake level (~856 ft) with an open view straight back across the water to the State Capitol dome — the single best sightline on the map. Continuously attractive to people for at least 12,000 years; six extant effigy mounds plus one destroyed by relic hunters. Farms here from the early 19th century; lumberman Edward Young bought it in 1924, expanded the farmhouse into a rambling 15-room mansion, planted an apple orchard and cut bridle paths that are today's walking trails, and built the distinctive stone entrance gateway. The house burned spectacularly in 1935; only a faint brick path remains under the leaf litter. Young's family sold to the university in 1941 for $230,000 plus a 33.5-acre land swap. Reservable fire circles along the walk; the tip is a ritual destination for sunrises, proposals and bonfires.
landmarks.game_idea: THE LONG POINT — a linear one-way peninsula route with no shortcuts: water on both sides, forest closing in, and a stone gateway at the neck that acts as the checkpoint. Fire circles function as campsites where you can rest, cook, and trigger night-only encounters. At the tip, a Legendary appears only at dawn and only when the far Capitol dome is visible (clear weather), making it a weather-and-time-gated capture. Buried under the trail: the burned mansion's brick path as a treasure-hunting layer.

landmarks.name: Muir Woods and Muir Knoll
landmarks.character: Seven acres of closed forest on the steep north-facing back slope of Bascom Hill, ~894 ft, formally John Muir Park, hemmed by Observatory Drive, Bascom Hall and the Sewell Social Sciences Building. Thousands of people pass within yards of it every day and most never enter — a secluded wood hidden in the busiest part of campus. Muir lived and studied in North Hall in the early 1860s, directly across the road; his dorm window looked at these trees, and he likely gathered firewood in them. Muir Knoll, the open knob designated in his honor in 1918, once carried a ski jump and toboggan run and now offers a lake view and a rustic staircase down through the woods to the Lakeshore Path.
landmarks.game_idea: THE HIDDEN WOOD — a secret area whose entrance is an unmarked rustic staircase behind the hill; easy to walk past a hundred times. Dense canopy means the minimap goes dark inside and you navigate by sound cues. It is the vertical shortcut between the high campus and the lakeshore — once found, it permanently links two otherwise distant zones. In winter, Muir Knoll reverts to its ski-jump past as a downhill sled minigame that launches you onto the lake ice.

landmarks.name: Observatory Hill and Washburn Observatory
landmarks.character: The western lobe of the same drumlin as Bascom Hill and the highest ground in the built campus at ~954–955 ft, ~105 ft above the lake. Washburn Observatory (1878) sits on the crest; the Observatory Drive Overlook is mid-slope. From here you look NW to Picnic Point and out across Lake Mendota to Madison's north and east sides — nearly the full extent of the preserve visible at once, and the standard graduation-photo backdrop. Observatory Drive itself is the ridge road, a notorious bike climb. A Paleo-Indian projectile point has been recovered from the hilltop.
landmarks.game_idea: THE OVERLOOK — the map-revealing vista point: standing at the summit unfogs the whole northwest quadrant and marks distant landmarks (Picnic Point, Eagle Heights, the far shore) as fast-travel targets. Washburn Observatory opens at night as a Psychic/Cosmic gym-adjacent puzzle where you aim the refractor at constellations to summon star-linked encounters. Daytime it's a photo-spot quest hub; Observatory Drive is a downhill bike time-trial back to the lakeshore.

landmarks.name: Observatory Hill Mound Group (effigy mounds)
landmarks.character: Two surviving Late Woodland effigy mounds, built roughly 650–1200 CE, on the crest between Washburn Observatory (1401 Observatory Dr) and Agriculture Hall/1450 Linden Dr, ~946 ft. One is a bird; the other is a double-tailed turtle or water spirit. At least five mounds once stood here — a panther effigy and a linear mound among those destroyed during campus construction in the 20th century. The site is under an acre and was added to the National Register on March 31, 2004. The Ho-Chunk Nation, on whose ancestral land this sits, hold themselves descendants of the mound builders. Three other groups survive on campus: Willow Drive (three effigies plus a conical, including a goose mound beside the Lakeshore Path north of the Natatorium), Picnic Point (six), and Eagle Heights (three). Tobacco offerings are still tied to trees nearby.
landmarks.game_idea: THE EARTHWORKS — sacred ground, and the game should treat it that way: you cannot battle, dig, or capture here, and stepping on a mound is refused outright. Instead it is a shrine mechanic — leave a respectful offering at the bird and the water-spirit mounds and a corresponding blessing activates (Flying-type and Water-type buffs). Finding all four surviving campus mound groups completes a quiet, combat-free questline narrated by a Ho-Chunk elder NPC, with the destroyed panther and linear mounds present only as absences on the map.

landmarks.name: Willow Creek and the Willow Creek delta
landmarks.character: A creek that has been straightened into an artificial channel; it was once broad, marshy and meandering. It drains a huge watershed — the west campus and much of Madison's west side, out almost to Whitney Way — and dumps stormwater sediment into University Bay, building a large visible delta plus a second offshore sandbar. The Lakeshore Path crosses on Willow Creek Bridge, originally built by the Madison Park and Pleasure Drive Association (commemorative plaque on the north side); it's a favorite fishing spot and a reliable place to see basking turtles. Creek mouth sits at lake level, 850 ft, just west of the Natatorium; the goose effigy mound is nearby on the path.
landmarks.game_idea: THE CHANNEL — a Water route with a pollution mechanic: the creek's encounter table is degraded (weak, sickly spawns) because of the sediment and runoff coming down from the west side. A multi-stage restoration questline — clearing the culvert, planting the banks, working with the city NPCs — progressively upgrades the water quality, and with it the rarity tier of what spawns in the delta. The bridge is a fishing spot with a turtle-basking timing minigame; the delta itself is walkable shallows that only appear at low water.

landmarks.name: University Bay, Class of 1918 Marsh and Willow Beach
landmarks.character: University Bay is the lake south and west of an imaginary line from the tip of Picnic Point to the Memorial Union Terrace. It used to be much larger, reaching west to today's University Bay Drive; wave action built a sandbar of lake sediment that cut the western lobe off, and that isolated remnant is now the Class of 1918 Marsh (~849 ft), restored starting 1969 by an environmental studies class with funds from the class's 50th reunion. The Lakeshore Path between Willow Creek and Picnic Point literally rides on that sandbar — you walk a geological feature. University Bay Marsh and Triangle Marsh (a northern pike nursery) sit alongside. Willow Beach, just east of the creek mouth at ~851 ft, is the swimming and boat-storage spot. Dabbling ducks work the bay edges; diving ducks, loons, grebes and tundra swans use the open water on spring and fall migration.
landmarks.game_idea: THE SANDBAR ROAD — a causeway route where land is actively being made: the path is a thin strip with marsh on one side and open bay on the other, and a second sandbar is visibly forming offshore that becomes walkable in a later chapter, opening a new mini-island. Seasonal migration event — twice a year the bay fills with rare Flying/Water migrants that are only catchable during the migration window. The Class of 1918 Marsh is a restoration project you can volunteer for, and pike nursery waters mean high-level Water predators lurking in the shallows.

landmarks.name: Howard Temin Lakeshore Path
landmarks.character: The eastern half of the Lakeshore Path (the western half is the Lake Mendota Path), running at lake level from the Memorial Union west past Alumni Park, the Hasler Laboratory of Limnology, the Natatorium and its goose mound, Willow Creek Bridge, Willow Beach, across the University Bay sandbar to the base of Picnic Point and on to Frautschi Point. Flat, near-continuous, and the connective tissue of the entire lakeshore — everything on the water hangs off it. Named for the Nobel laureate virologist. Bikes, runners, and a lakeward view the entire way.
landmarks.game_idea: THE LAKE ROAD — the region's main artery route, deliberately flat and fast (bike bonus movement) in contrast to the climbs everywhere else, with every lakeshore landmark hung off it as a branch. Encounters change every few hundred meters as you pass beach, creek mouth, marsh and sandbar. Running the full length end-to-end under a time limit is a recurring race event against a rival; the reward is a permanent speed upgrade.

landmarks.name: Frautschi Point, Second Point Woods and Biocore Prairie
landmarks.character: The northernmost land in the preserve, ~890 ft, with the most diverse tree species and bird life. Second Point Woods behind it is old farm field regenerating into forest, and Biocore Prairie (~926 ft) is a restored tallgrass prairie on former cropland, run as a student research site. Tent Colony Woods to the west was Camp Gallistella, a university summer tent colony from 1912 to 1962. Bill's Woods and Caretaker's Woods (8 acres of shade vegetation) fill in between. This stretch is quiet, hilly, and genuinely remote-feeling despite being a mile from a stadium.
landmarks.game_idea: THE REGROWING FIELDS — a succession zone whose encounter table changes with in-game time as the old farm fields turn back into forest: early game it's prairie and grassland species, late game the same map spawns woodland types. Biocore Prairie hosts a controlled-burn event that temporarily converts it to a Fire-type habitat and resets rare spawns. Tent Colony Woods holds the ruins of a vanished summer camp — a night-only ghost-story sidequest with 1912–1962 flavor.

landmarks.name: Eagle Heights (apartments and Eagle Heights Woods)
landmarks.character: The far northwest corner and the top of the map. Eagle Heights Woods is 28 acres of oak forest on a bluff standing about 150 ft above Lake Mendota, and its summit (~1,005 ft per the university; DEM reads 994–1,012 ft) is the highest point on campus — the total relief across the whole 936-acre campus is only 155 ft, from 850 ft at the University Bay shoreline to 1,005 ft here. Three burial mounds sit on the bluff top, one hemispherical and two linear, built perhaps a thousand years ago, all visible from the loop trail; walking on them is prohibited. The Ho-Chunk name recorded for the hill is Sho-heta-ka, horse hill: a spirit horse was said to live on the highest hill on Lake Mendota's shore, heard neighing and stamping, sometimes glimpsed on misty days, and people came here to fast and dream and draw power from it. Tobacco offerings still appear tied to the trees. Below the woods, Eagle Heights is a 1,050-apartment village for graduate students, postdocs, staff and families set in 83 acres of green space, with large community gardens — the most internationally diverse residential community on the map.
landmarks.game_idea: SHO-HETA-KA, HORSE HILL — the endgame summit. The bluff-top loop is the final climb of the region, and on misty or overcast days only, a Legendary spirit horse (Ghost/Fairy or Ghost/Ground) manifests on the highest ground. You cannot fight it: you must camp on the summit, fast overnight (no items used for a full in-game day) and dream, and it appears in the dream sequence — a vision-quest encounter rather than a battle. The three mounds are untouchable shrines that must each receive an offering first. Below, the Eagle Heights village is the region's most cosmopolitan trading hub — global NPC residents offer species from far-off regions, and the community gardens are the best berry-trading market in the game.

landmarks.name: Raymer's Cove
landmarks.character: A small sand cove and beach at the base of the wooded bluff on the far west lakeshore, ~852 ft, reached by a long stair descent from Lake Mendota Drive. The shoreline here is raw bluff face rather than seawall — this is where the campus stops being architecture and becomes coast. Sunset viewpoint.
landmarks.game_idea: THE COVE — a hidden beach reached only by a long descending staircase, cut off from the path network above. Because it faces west it is the only reliable sunset-triggered spawn location; certain Fairy/Water evolutions only trigger while standing here at dusk. Message-in-a-bottle items wash up daily, carrying coordinates to other locations on the map.

landmarks.name: Alumni Park and the Hasler Laboratory of Limnology
landmarks.character: The seam between the Terrace and the Lakeshore Path, ~864 ft: a landscaped commemorative lawn stepping down to the water, with the Arthur D. Hasler Laboratory of Limnology next door at 680 N Park St. Lake Mendota has been called the most-studied lake in the United States, and this is where that study happens — 9,740 acres of surface, 12.8 m mean and 25.3 m maximum depth, 21.6 miles of shoreline, with an ice-on/ice-off record kept since the 1850s.
landmarks.game_idea: THE LIMNOLOGY LAB — the region's Pokédex research annex, specialized in aquatic life. Hand in water samples collected from each distinct body on the map (open lake, bay, marsh, creek, cove) and the professor unlocks depth-tier encounters — you can only reach the deep-water 83 ft species after upgrading your diving gear here. A century-and-a-half ice record on the wall is the in-game climate log that predicts when the lake will freeze, which gates the winter ice-walking routes.

notes:
ELEVATION AND RELIEF (the map's vertical structure). Campus total relief is small but concentrated: the university's own figure is 155 ft across 936 acres, from 850 ft at the Lake Mendota shoreline in University Bay (the lowest point, and the lake's surface elevation) to 1,005 ft at Eagle Heights Woods (the highest point on campus, per UW alumni sources). I cross-checked every location against the USGS 1/3 arc-second (10 m) NED via OpenTopoData; those readings agree closely with published figures and are the source of the "~ft" numbers in each entry (Bascom Hall 951 ft, Observatory Hill/Washburn 954-955 ft, Muir Woods 894 ft, Van Hise 924 ft, Allen Garden 875 ft, Babcock 871 ft, Engineering Hall 875 ft, Union South 873 ft, Camp Randall 866 ft, Chazen 867 ft, Memorial Union 869 ft, Library Mall 861 ft, Alumni Park 864 ft, Willow Beach 851 ft, Willow Creek 850 ft, Class of 1918 Marsh 849 ft, Picnic Point tip 856 ft, Frautschi Point 890 ft, Biocore Prairie 926 ft, Eagle Heights 994-1012 ft). An earlier ASTER 30 m pass ran ~30 ft high throughout and was discarded.

Bascom Hill is a real hill and should be modeled as one. The authoritative figure from the Wisconsin Alumni Association: 86 ft of gain over 850 ft of run from the Park Street sidewalk to the base of the Lincoln statue, about a 10 percent grade / 5.8 degrees. That is a hard walk with a backpack and an unwalkable sheet of ice in winter. Crucially, the Lakeshore Nature Preserve states that Bascom Hill and Observatory Hill are NOT two hills but two lobes of a single glacial drumlin laid down ~12,000 years ago (Wikipedia's Bascom Hill article instead calls it one of two drumlins; I flag the discrepancy rather than resolving it). Practical map consequence: there is one continuous high ridge running WNW from Bascom Hall through Van Hise and Observatory Hill, with Observatory Drive as the ridge road, and it drops steeply on its north face into Muir Woods and then to the lake. So the campus reads as three bands - a flat downtown edge at 860 ft (Library Mall, Chazen, State Street), a ridge at 950-955 ft, and a flat lakeshore at 850-870 ft on the far side. Eagle Heights is a separate, higher bluff 3 miles west, standing ~150 ft above the water.

HOW CAMPUS MEETS LAKE MENDOTA. Three distinct shoreline types, east to west. (1) Hardened/architectural: at Memorial Union the building's flagstone Terrace steps directly to a seawall and piers, with no beach - the only place the built campus touches open water. Alumni Park and the Limnology Lab continue this for a few hundred yards. (2) Path-on-sandbar: from Willow Creek west to the base of Picnic Point, the Howard Temin Lakeshore Path runs at lake level on a wave-built sandbar of lake sediment. University Bay was once much larger, reaching west to today's University Bay Drive; the sandbar isolated its western lobe, which is now the Class of 1918 Marsh (restored from 1969 by a class-funded student project). A second sandbar is currently forming offshore, fed by the Willow Creek delta - the shoreline here is actively growing, which is a gift for a game map that changes between chapters. (3) Wooded bluff: from Picnic Point west through Frautschi Point, Tent Colony Woods and Raymer's Cove to Eagle Heights, the land rises into forested bluffs up to 150 ft, with sand coves at the base. Picnic Point itself is a nearly mile-long peninsula whose tip is only ~6 ft above the lake and sights straight back across the water to the State Capitol dome. Winter matters: Mendota freezes most years and the ice sheet becomes walkable, which turns the lake from a barrier into a traversable surface and inverts the whole map's connectivity for one season.

EFFIGY MOUNDS AND FIRST NATIONS CONTEXT - handle with care in any game treatment. Four Late Woodland mound groups survive on campus, built roughly 650-1200 CE: Observatory Hill (bird plus double-tailed turtle/water spirit; at least five originally, a panther and a linear mound destroyed in the 20th century; NRHP-listed 31 March 2004, ref 04000255), Willow Drive (three effigies plus a conical, including a goose mound beside the Lakeshore Path north of the Natatorium), Picnic Point (six extant, a seventh destroyed by relic hunters), and Eagle Heights (three - one hemispherical, two linear, on the bluff summit). These are burial mounds and active sacred sites; tobacco offerings are still tied to trees at Eagle Heights and Ho-Chunk prayer bundles are placed there. The Ho-Chunk Nation, whose ancestral land this is (their name for the Four Lakes region is rendered Ta-ko-per-ah), hold themselves descendants of the mound builders. My design recommendation, reflected in the entries: make mounds no-battle, no-dig, no-capture shrine zones with an offering/blessing mechanic and a quiet non-combat questline, never dungeons or loot sites. The Eagle Heights spirit-horse legend (Sho-heta-ka, "horse hill," recorded by Charles E. Brown in 1927) is documented on the university's own preserve site and is the strongest available hook for a respectful legendary encounter.

SOURCING AND COORDINATE CONFIDENCE. All coordinates were pulled from OpenStreetMap via Nominatim (named nodes/ways for each feature) except the Observatory Hill Mound Group, which comes from its Wikipedia NRHP coordinates (43 deg 04'34"N 89 deg 24'36"W). All are marked "verified"; none were estimated or invented. Where a feature is linear or areal (Willow Creek, the Lakeshore Path, the Lakeshore Nature Preserve, Bascom Hill) the coordinate is OSM's representative point on that feature, not a precise centroid - fine for map placement, not for surveying. Facts come from lakeshorepreserve.wisc.edu (the richest single source, and the origin of the drumlin, University Bay sandbar, Willow Creek, Muir Woods, Eagle Heights and Picnic Point history material), union.wisc.edu and news.wisc.edu, uwalumni.com (Bascom Hill grade; campus elevation extremes), babcockdairystore.wisc.edu, and Wikipedia (Bascom Hill, Memorial Union, Camp Randall Stadium, Chazen, Lake Mendota, Lakeshore Nature Preserve, Observatory Hill Mound Group).

ONE LIVE CHANGE WORTH KNOWING. The engineering campus is mid-transformation: 1410 Engineering Drive is being demolished for a $419M, 395,000 sq ft engineering center spanning part of Engineering Mall, groundbreaking already done. Library Mall also has a ~$6M redesign proposed that would replace the 1958 Hagenah Fountain with interactive sprays. Both are good excuses for a map that visibly rebuilds itself between acts.

area: Madison, Wisconsin — Near East Side & Yahara River corridor, plus the Near West Side (Regent/Monroe/Vilas/Hilldale)
biomes: urban isthmus / dense walkable streetcar neighborhood
freshwater lake shoreline (Mendota & Monona)
channelized river corridor with locks and parkway
restored prairie and oak savanna edges
cattail marsh and creek wetland (Starkweather)
post-industrial brownfield / adaptive-reuse factory district
rail-to-trail greenway corridor
cultivated botanical garden and conservatory (tropical microbiome)
college-town commercial strip

highway interchange badlands (Beltline)
