landmarks.name: Williamson Street (Willy Street)
landmarks.character: The spine and soul of the near east side. Settled by 19th-century German immigrants who built taverns, shops and churches along Williamson and Jenifer Streets; by the 1970s it was Madison's counterculture haven — co-ops, radicals, hippies, cheap rent. The Marquette Neighborhood Association (formed 1959, Madison's first) still runs a dense calendar of street culture: the Willy Street Fair, La Fete de Marquette, Orton Park Festival, the Waterfront Festival. Narrow, pedestrian- and bike-first, lined with mismatched frame houses, murals, worker cottages and storefront bars. Now visibly gentrifying and openly anxious about it — new condos next to 130-year-old cream-brick buildings, and a running argument about whether the street can go upscale and stay weird. Runs roughly from the Capitol end at Blair Street southeast to the Yahara River.
landmarks.game_idea: The first true 'town' route after the starter area: a long, narrow, one-screen-wide street where every doorway is enterable and no two are alike. NPCs here trade rather than battle — a co-op that swaps berries and held items by weight, a tattooist who re-styles your Pokemon's markings, a bookshop with move tutors hiding in the stacks. Once per in-game year the Willy Street Fair takes over the map: the road closes, the tile set changes to stages and food carts, and a rotating roster of eccentric one-off trainers (the Drum Circle, the Stilt-Walker, the Puppet Brigade) appears for that day only. Fairy, Normal and Grass types dominate; a recurring 'Keep It Weird' NPC faction quietly opposes the developer faction that shows up in the mid-game.

landmarks.name: Willy Street Co-op (East)
landmarks.character: 1221 Williamson Street. The cooperative grocery that gave the street half its identity and is the practical anchor of daily life in Marquette — bulk bins, member-owners, a community bulletin board that functions as the neighborhood's nervous system.
landmarks.game_idea: The region's Mart replacement: a member-owned depot where prices drop as your 'membership' reputation rises, and where consumables are sold in bulk (buy 10 berries at a discount rather than one at a time). The bulletin board outside is the quest board — pinned index cards give small fetch, escort and lost-Pokemon jobs that refresh weekly.

landmarks.name: Third Lake Ridge Historic District / Marquette Neighborhood
landmarks.character: Madison's second locally designated historic district (Common Council, 1979), covering the oldest part of Marquette: Blair Street east to the Yahara River, Williamson Street south to Lake Monona. A deliberate mix of industrial, commercial and residential fabric — workers' cottages, corner taverns, small factories — preserved after the neighborhood association asked for protection as part of its own revitalization plan. 'Third Lake' is the old settler name for Lake Monona.
landmarks.game_idea: A protected old-quarter sub-district where the tile art shifts to weathered cream brick and clapboard and a Preservation Society NPC blocks any attempt to shortcut through. Ghost- and Steel-types nest in the shuttered small factories; an optional sidequest has you photographing twelve specific historic facades for a local archivist, unlocking a key item that reveals hidden doors in old buildings region-wide.

landmarks.name: Yahara River Parkway (Mendota–Monona channel)
landmarks.character: The engineered heart of the isthmus. The Yahara (62 miles total, originally called the Catfish River) once meandered through marsh and bottomland between the lakes; settlers dumped garbage on its banks and it was straightened into a canal by 1905. Ossian Cole Simonds — the father of Prairie School landscape architecture — designed the parkway that frames it, built 1900–1911. About one mile of no-wake water crossing the isthmus, with roughly eleven bridges over that single mile, backyard fences on one side and boulevard lawns on the other. Lake Mendota sits about five feet above Lake Monona.
landmarks.game_idea: A vertical-scrolling water route that connects the two great lake zones, playable only once you have Surf. Because it is engineered, it is unnaturally straight — a corridor of eleven bridges, each a discrete arena where a trainer waits above you and throws down as you pass beneath. Water/Flying types (herons, kingfishers) patrol; the trash-strewn history is a Poison-type sub-theme, with a cleanup sidequest that visibly changes the water tiles from murky to clear and raises encounter quality along the whole corridor.

landmarks.name: Tenney Park Lock and Dam (Tenney Locks)
landmarks.character: Where the Yahara leaves Lake Mendota. Leonard Farwell built the first earthen dam here in 1847 to power the Madison Mills, raising Mendota several feet, drowning wetlands and enraging shoreline owners; a thunderstorm destroyed it on 4 April 1866. The city bought the site in 1896, added a boat lock and concrete; the modern locks were built in 1904 for the motorboat boom — 612 boats passed through in a single day in 1913. Rebuilt in 1959 on a closed landfill, operated by Dane County since 1981, upgraded 2006. The largest of three locks on the Yahara; roughly 10,000 boats a year lock through a five-foot drop.
landmarks.game_idea: A puzzle gate, not a battle. The lock is a water-level machine: flood and drain the chamber to raise or lower your raft between the high Mendota tier and the low Monona tier, and use the same mechanic to expose or submerge side channels holding items and rare encounters. The Lockmaster is an old Water-type specialist who won't open the gate until you've proven you can control water yourself. Deep in the chamber, on the old landfill fill, a Poison/Steel encounter lurks — the buried past of the dam. Thematic ties: 1847, 1866 flood, 1904, 1913.

landmarks.name: Tenney Park
landmarks.character: Simonds-designed Prairie School park at the Mendota end of the Yahara corridor, with lagoons, arched stone footbridges, a beach and, in winter, one of the city's great outdoor skating rinks. Formal, curvilinear, deliberately picturesque — the polished counterpart to the working locks beside it.
landmarks.game_idea: A seasonal dual-state area. In summer it is a lagoon maze of islands and arched bridges where Water and Bug types breed; in winter the lagoons freeze into a single Ice-type skating field with sliding-puzzle movement (you glide until you hit an obstacle) and a completely different encounter table. Both states must be cleared to get the park's hidden item.

landmarks.name: Yahara Place Park
landmarks.character: The Monona-end bookend of the river corridor — a narrow green shelf where the Yahara empties into Lake Monona, on the edge between Marquette and Schenk's Corners. Big shade trees, a long shoreline path, informal paddle launch, one of the best sunset-over-the-lake views on the east side. Quiet, unprogrammed, locals-only in feel.
landmarks.game_idea: The calm landing after the eleven-bridge gauntlet: a save point and healing spot with no wild encounters on land, and the region's paddle-rental NPC who unlocks free-roam surfing on Lake Monona. A daily Sunset window (in-game clock) makes a rare Fairy/Water encounter appear on the water just offshore — the only place and time it spawns.

landmarks.name: Schenk's Corners (Atwood Avenue & Winnebago Street)
landmarks.character: The old crossroads market of the east side. The Schenk family opened a saloon on the corner, then a general store and a grocery, serving farmers coming into Madison to sell produce and stocking up on the way home; by the mid-20th century it was a full traditional shopping district. Blue-collar for generations, it re-emerged in the 2000s as the funkiest node of the creative class — restaurants, cafes, art studios, tattoo shops, a handful of stubborn dive bars, all packed into an awkward five-way junction.
landmarks.game_idea: A hub crossroads with five exits, deliberately confusing on first visit — the map screen shows it as a star. Each spoke leads to a different sub-district and each corner building is a different service: the old saloon is now the battle-tutor bar, the general store is the item-refurbisher, the art studio does cosmetic Pokemon customization. A ghost of the original saloon appears at night in the upstairs window; talk to it three separate nights for the district's key item.

landmarks.name: Atwood Avenue
landmarks.character: The main street of the Schenk-Atwood-Starkweather-Yahara neighborhood, running northeast from Schenk's Corners toward Olbrich. Locally owned end to end, exceptionally walkable and bikeable, anchored by the Barrymore Theatre and terminating at Olbrich Gardens. Less studenty and more settled than Willy Street — families, tradespeople, artists, and a strong shop-local ethic.
landmarks.game_idea: The second town strip, structurally a mirror of Willy Street but calmer and more residential: fewer shops, more houses whose doors you can knock on, more overworld NPCs who remember you between visits. It functions as the region's 'reputation' street — helping specific residents across the mid-game unlocks a block-party endgame event that grants access to the Barrymore's hidden back room.

landmarks.name: Barrymore Theatre
landmarks.character: 2090 Atwood Avenue. A 1929 atmospheric movie palace turned independent music hall — domed ceiling painted as a night sky, ornate proscenium, sticky floors, the east side's living room for concerts, comedy and weird one-off shows.
landmarks.game_idea: A performance-hall gym or battle venue where the ceiling is a working starfield: the painted constellations rotate with the in-game clock, and battles fought under specific constellations get type-boosted (a Dark boost under the new moon, a Fairy boost under a named star). The house band NPCs each carry one Pokemon that only knows sound-based moves. Beating the venue's headliner earns a TM for a music-themed move.

landmarks.name: Goodman Community Center (Ironworks & Brassworks)
landmarks.character: Two salvaged factories turned into one civic engine on Waubesa Street. The Ironworks building — a heavy-timber one-story production shed, 80 by 180 feet, with ground-floor windows and two rows of high clerestory windows for light and air — housed the American Shredder Company and, from 1906, the Steinle Turret Lathe Machine Company; it is on the National Register. The Brassworks (built 1918, additions through 1959) was Madison Brass Works, founded 1907 by Henry W. Vogts and Edward G. Schwenn, sand-casting brass, bronze and aluminum for Madison, Milwaukee, Racine and Chicago until it closed in 1994 — and in 1911 it cast the bronze 'Sifting and Winnowing' plaque that hangs at the entrance of Bascom Hall. Listed on the National Register in 2016 after Goodman bought it. Today: food pantry, teen programs, after-school care, senior lunches, gym, the neighborhood's safety net and its rec center at once.
landmarks.game_idea: The region's community hub building — free healing, a daycare that actually raises your Pokemon while you're away, a food pantry that converts surplus berries into supplies for NPCs (a giving mechanic that raises regional reputation), and a teen trainers' league you can coach: pick three local kids, train them across the game, and they show up in the endgame as allies. In the Brassworks foundry basement, a Steel-type sub-dungeon lets you cast a bronze plaque of your own — a key item whose inscription changes based on choices you made, echoing 'Sifting and Winnowing'.

landmarks.name: Garver Feed Mill
landmarks.character: The 'sugar castle.' Built 1906 by the United States Sugar Company as a sugar beet processing plant — 200,000 square feet, about $600,000, the largest factory ever built in Madison at the time, with Romanesque arches and a four-story tower. The sugar operation closed in 1924; James R. Garver bought it in 1930 for Garver's Supply Company, which ran until 1997. Then two decades of spectacular decay — a legendary urban-exploration ruin at the edge of Olbrich. Baum Revision bought it in December 2017; an 18-month, roughly $15.5 million renovation inside a $19.8 million project reopened it in 2019 as a food and wellness hall: bakery, ice cream, mushroom farm, kombucha, event hall, all under the original arches.
landmarks.game_idea: The signature dungeon of the east side, and a two-state location. Visit it early and it is the ruined 'Sugar Castle' — collapsed roof, Ghost and Bug types, vine-choked Romanesque arcades, a four-story tower climb with a boss at the top. Complete the restoration questline (gathering materials and convincing investor NPCs) and it converts permanently into a bustling food-hall hub with vendors, cooking/berry-blending stations and a mushroom cultivator who breeds Grass/Fairy types in the old cold cellars. The Sugar theme runs through both states: sweet lures attract rare spawns here that they attract nowhere else, and the sugar-beet ghosts drop candy-class items.

landmarks.name: Olbrich Botanical Gardens & Royal Thai Pavilion
landmarks.character: Sixteen acres of outdoor gardens plus the Bolz Conservatory glass pyramid, envisioned by Michael Olbrich in 1916 and realized in 1952 under John Olin's design. The Royal Thai Pavilion — a gift from the Thai government and the Thai chapter of the Wisconsin Alumni Association to UW–Madison, which passed it to the city — was built in Thailand of plantation teak with no nails or screws, shipped seven weeks by sea, railed to Chicago, trucked to Madison, and reassembled in three weeks by nine Thai artisans in September 2001. It is the only Thai pavilion in the continental United States, sited here for the garden setting and the nearness of water. It stands on the east bank of Starkweather Creek just south of the Capital City Trail bridge.
landmarks.game_idea: A tropical microbiome dropped into a cold region: the glass conservatory is an interior route with a permanent Sunny/humid weather state, hosting Grass, Bug and Fire encounters found nowhere else on the map, plus orchid-themed rare spawns. The Thai Pavilion is a shrine — gilded, water-surrounded, joinery-perfect — where a Fairy/Psychic guardian legendary can be woken only by performing the correct offering ritual, and where a puzzle involves reassembling a structure with no fasteners (fit the pieces by shape, not by force). A gardener NPC gives out seeds that grow different berries depending on which garden bed you plant them in.

landmarks.name: Olbrich Park
landmarks.character: The lakefront half of the Olbrich complex — a broad municipal park on the northeast shore of Lake Monona where Starkweather Creek empties in. Beach and boat launch, ball diamonds, big open lawn, a paddle-rental operation (Rutabaga) putting kayaks, canoes and SUPs on the water, and a Capital City Trail trailhead. Where the east side actually touches its lake.
landmarks.game_idea: The open-water gateway and the region's fishing/surfing hub: rent a craft here to unlock free navigation of Lake Monona, with encounter tables that change by distance from shore and by weather. The creek mouth is a distinct micro-zone where lake and creek species mix — the only place both tables roll at once, making it the spot for rare hybrids. A summer beach festival event brings a rotating gauntlet of visiting trainers.

landmarks.name: Starkweather Creek & Path
landmarks.character: A tributary reaching from the airport down to Olbrich Park and east to Reiner Road, entering Lake Monona at the lake's northeast corner. Long treated as an industrial back-drain, now a Friends-group restoration cause; the three-mile Starkweather Creek Path branches off the Capital City Trail near the Goodman Community Center and traces the water north through Starkweather, Worthington Park, Eken Park and Carpenter-Ridgeway. Cattails, herons, culverts, graffiti under the bridges — genuinely wild in stretches, unmistakably urban in others.
landmarks.game_idea: A marsh route with a contamination mechanic: the creek's pollution level is a tracked stat, and Poison/Water types dominate until you complete restoration objectives that shift the table toward Bug, Grass and Flying. The path is a linear branch route with culvert tunnels as small dark dungeons. Herons here are the region's fast, fragile Flying line; a hidden legendary guards the headwaters near the airport, reachable only at low contamination.

landmarks.name: Capital City State Trail
landmarks.character: Seventeen miles of paved trail from Cottage Grove Road on the east side to the Southwest Madison Bike Interchange at Arrowhead Park in Fitchburg, run by the Wisconsin DNR. It follows a rail corridor into the center of the city, runs the Lake Monona shoreline, passes through Frank Lloyd Wright's Monona Terrace, ducks under the Beltline and enters the Nine Springs E-Way with prairie, wetland and forest. A state trail pass is required for the nine-mile Capital Springs stretch. Trailheads at Olin and Olbrich Parks. A downtown counter logged about 1,400 riders a day in 2023.
landmarks.game_idea: The region's connective spine — a long cycling route that replaces walking speed with a bike gear, links five otherwise separate zones, and passes through every biome in sequence (urban, lakeshore, tunnel, prairie, wetland). Trail-pass gating gives a natural mid-game barrier: you can ride the free stretch from the start but need the DNR pass to reach the prairie half. Rolling trainer encounters happen at speed — you must engage or outrun them — and a daily rider-count NPC pays out escalating rewards the more of the trail you cover in one session.

landmarks.name: Southwest Commuter Path
landmarks.character: 5.6 miles of former rail corridor from Brittingham Park on Lake Monona out to the Capital City State Trail at Arrowhead Park in Fitchburg, cutting behind Camp Randall, along the back of Dudgeon-Monroe and out past the Beltline. Sunken below street grade in places, walled with murals and retaining walls, connecting to the Cannonball Path. The near west side's real main street for anyone on two wheels.
landmarks.game_idea: A trench route: the path runs below the city, so the buildings and streets you know are visible above you but unreachable, and stairways up to the surface act as one-way shortcuts you unlock as you go. Being sunken makes it dark and Poison/Dark-flavored at night. The mural walls are a collectible set — photograph all of them for a cosmetic reward. It is the fastest traverse of the near west side once opened, and it physically links the Vilas/Monroe cluster to the Beltline zone.

landmarks.name: Regent Street
landmarks.character: A contested mile between Camp Randall Stadium and the Kohl Center — currently disjointed, hard on pedestrians, and in the middle of a fight over a redesign. This is the last standing fragment of the Greenbush, the Italian, Jewish and Black immigrant neighborhood largely erased by urban renewal; much of what survives is concentrated in the 800 and 900 blocks. Today it is student bars, coffee shops, hospital workers, game-day crowds, longtime institutions like Greenbush Bakery, and new mid-rise construction closing in. Planners talk explicitly about not cleansing what little old-world vibe remains.
landmarks.game_idea: A route in visible transition — half the tiles are construction hoarding, and the map literally changes between visits as blocks get redeveloped. A branching civic questline lets you side with the developers or with the Greenbush preservation NPCs; your choice permanently determines which buildings exist in the late game and which of two rival trainer factions you can recruit from. On football Saturdays the street floods with a red-clad crowd that blocks movement and spawns a mob of low-level 'fan' trainers you must weave through. Fighting- and Normal-types; an elderly baker NPC hands out a restorative item found nowhere else.

landmarks.name: Camp Randall Stadium
landmarks.character: The University of Wisconsin's football stadium at 1440 Monroe Street, on the grounds of a Civil War training camp — 80,000-plus people, a stadium that physically shakes, and the anchor that makes the whole Regent/Monroe corridor pulse on autumn weekends.
landmarks.game_idea: A colosseum-style battle facility: a tiered tournament with a live crowd meter that buffs whichever trainer the audience favors, so showy moves and quick knockouts matter as much as damage. Between rounds the Civil War camp history surfaces as a night-only Ghost-type encounter under the stands. Winning the top bracket grants a stadium-only title and a Fighting-type TM.

landmarks.name: Monroe Street
landmarks.character: Wisconsin's first public road — Monroe Road — commercial since the 1850s and continuously so for nearly two centuries. About a mile of locally owned shops, bakeries, ice cream, restaurants and boutiques threaded through quiet residential blocks between Camp Randall and Glenway, serving the Dudgeon-Monroe and Vilas neighborhoods. Prosperous, low-rise, family-scaled, tree-canopied — the polite, well-kept counterweight to Willy Street's scruff.
landmarks.game_idea: The affluent shopping route: the region's high-end vendors cluster here (rare held items, custom Poke Ball artisan, a confectioner whose treats permanently raise a friendship stat), with prices to match. As the oldest road in the region, it hosts a historical questline — follow the original 1850s road alignment through modern backyards and alleys to reach a buried waystone. Low wild-encounter density, high NPC density; a good mid-game economy zone rather than a combat zone.

landmarks.name: Vilas Neighborhood (Henry Vilas Park, Zoo & Lake Wingra)
landmarks.character: Grew out of the Wingra Park Addition, platted 1889 as the first of Madison's 'suburbs' for people fleeing the crowded isthmus; the 1897 streetcar extension down Breese Terrace to Monroe Street made the lots desirable. Victorian, Queen Anne, Craftsman, Georgian Revival and Tudor houses under heavy tree cover, wrapped around Henry Vilas Park on Lake Wingra — with the free Henry Vilas Zoo at its center, a beach, lagoons and a small-town feel where the businesses are all within walking distance.
landmarks.game_idea: A zoo-and-lagoon zone that doubles as the region's Pokedex annex: the free zoo lets you view species from other regions you haven't caught, filling 'seen' entries and unlocking trade requests for each. Lake Wingra is a shallow spring-fed lake with a distinct calm-water encounter table from the big lakes. The historic streetcar line survives as a rideable heritage tram connecting Vilas to Monroe Street and Camp Randall. Architecture-loving NPCs run a house-tour sidequest across five named styles.

landmarks.name: Hilldale
landmarks.character: Broke ground 1961, opened 25 October 1962 on what was then the western edge of Madison, on University Hill Farms land the UW Regents sold off in the early 1950s; Kelab Inc. was formed in 1958 to run the 33-acre center, originally anchored by Milwaukee's Schuster's. Open-air walkways at first, enclosed as a mall in the late 1960s, then 'un-malled' in 2007 with an exterior street, new shops and parking garages. Never a normal mall and never quite mainstream — it keeps reinventing itself, and now reads as an open-air lifestyle district with apartments and offices grafted on, at the seam between the near west side and the suburbs.
landmarks.game_idea: A layered ruin-and-renewal dungeon: the current open-air center sits directly on top of the sealed 1960s enclosed mall, and a service door leads down into that abandoned interior — dead escalators, dark Schuster's shell, Ghost and Steel types, and a boss built from the mall's dead anchor store. Above ground it is a clean, bright commercial zone with the region's fashion/cosmetic vendors and a department-store battle challenge floor by floor. The historical throughline — farm to mall to lifestyle center — makes it the natural place for a time-travel or memory sequence showing all three states of the same ground.

landmarks.name: The Madison Beltline
landmarks.character: Approved in concept by the State Highway Commission in 1944, with construction starting in 1949 on the south Beltline and east Beltline (Stoughton Road). Park Street became an interchange in 1951, John Nolen in 1952; four-laning west of Mineral Point came in 1988–89, and the South Beltline to I-90 in 1989. Carries US 12, 14, 18 and 151 from the US 12/14 interchange in Middleton east to I-39/90. Built as a bypass, but by 2012 the city had grown past and around it, turning it into a congested urban freeway — a hard wall of noise, embankments and interchanges separating the old city from the newer south and west.
landmarks.game_idea: The region's great barrier: an impassable multi-lane freeway that walls off the southern half of the map. It cannot be crossed on foot — only through the specific underpasses where the Capital City Trail and Southwest Commuter Path duck beneath it, making those two trails into required keys rather than optional shortcuts. The underpasses themselves are dark, echoing Steel/Poison micro-dungeons with a permanent traffic-roar ambience that suppresses low-level encounters and attracts one specific noise-loving species. Crossing it for the first time is the mid-game gate that opens the outer region.

notes:
FACT SOURCING: Coordinates marked "verified" come from OpenStreetMap Nominatim lookups performed during this task, or from Wikipedia's own infobox coordinates (Capital City State Trail eastern terminus at Cottage Grove Road, 43.04222 / -89.36444). Coordinates marked "rough" are derived — Schenk's Corners is interpolated between verified Atwood Avenue and Winnebago Street segment points because the five-way junction itself is not a discrete OSM node; Third Lake Ridge is a district centroid estimate within its stated bounds (Blair St to the Yahara River, Williamson St to Lake Monona); Starkweather Creek's mouth is estimated just north of the verified Olbrich Park point; the Beltline point is a real verified OSM point on West Beltline Highway but represents a ~25-mile corridor, so it is flagged rough rather than treated as the feature's location. No coordinates were invented.

KEY GEOGRAPHIC STRUCTURE FOR THE MAP: The whole design hangs on Madison's isthmus. Lake Mendota (north, ~5 ft higher) and Lake Monona (south) are separated by a narrow neck of land, and the Yahara River is the only water connection — channelized straight across the isthmus by 1905, about one mile long with roughly eleven bridges, gated at the north end by the Tenney Locks. That gives you a natural high-tier/low-tier water system with a lock as the transition mechanic. Near east side landmarks arrange as a legible west-to-east chain along the Monona shore: Williamson St -> Yahara River crossing -> Schenk's Corners -> Atwood Ave -> Goodman Community Center -> Garver Feed Mill -> Olbrich Gardens/Park -> Starkweather Creek mouth. That chain is roughly 2.5 miles and reads as one continuous walkable route. Note that Garver, Goodman and Olbrich all sit adjacent to each other around the Capital City Trail, so they naturally form a single dungeon cluster rather than three separate stops.

NEAR WEST SIDE STRUCTURE: Regent Street, Monroe Street and Vilas form a tight triangle around Camp Randall Stadium, all within about a mile, with Lake Wingra as the southern water body (a third, smaller lake distinct from Mendota and Monona). Hilldale sits notably further west (~2.5 miles from Camp Randall) and functions as an outlying node, not part of the walkable cluster. The Southwest Commuter Path physically links Brittingham Park through this whole cluster and out under the Beltline — it is the only continuous connector between the near west side and the southern map.

RECOMMENDED GAME-MAP TOPOLOGY: Use the two bike trails as the spine. The Capital City State Trail (17 mi, east side to Fitchburg) and the Southwest Commuter Path (5.6 mi, Brittingham to Arrowhead Park) meet at Arrowhead Park, forming a loop that ties east and west sides together and is the only way past the Beltline barrier. This gives a clean progression gate: on foot you are confined to the isthmus; gain the bike and the trails open; gain the state trail pass and the prairie/Nine Springs half of the region opens.

THEMATIC PAIRINGS WORTH KEEPING: (1) Adaptive reuse is the dominant east-side motif — Garver (1906 sugar factory -> 2019 food hall), Goodman (1906 lathe works + 1918 brass foundry -> community center), Barrymore (1929 movie palace -> music hall), Hilldale (1962 open-air -> enclosed mall -> un-malled). Two-state locations (ruin vs restored) are strongly supported by real history in every one of these. (2) Water engineering vs. natural water — the straightened Yahara and the Tenney dam against the restored Starkweather Creek and Lake Wingra. (3) Preservation vs. development is a live, documented civic conflict on both Williamson Street and Regent Street, and would work as a single region-wide faction system rather than two unrelated sidequests.

DATES USABLE AS PUZZLE/LORE NUMBERS: 1847 (first Yahara dam), 1866 (dam destroyed by storm, April 4), 1889 (Wingra Park platted), 1897 (streetcar to Monroe St), 1904 (Tenney Locks built), 1905 (river straightened), 1906 (Garver sugar plant; Steinle Turret Lathe), 1911 ('Sifting and Winnowing' plaque cast at Madison Brass Works), 1913 (612 boats through the locks in one day), 1924 (sugar plant closes), 1944/1949 (Beltline approved/started), 1959 (Marquette Neighborhood Association founded; locks rebuilt), 1962 (Hilldale opens Oct 25), 1979 (Third Lake Ridge designated), 1997 (Garver's closes), 2001 (Thai Pavilion reassembled, September), 2019 (Garver reopens).

GAPS / THINGS I COULD NOT VERIFY: I could not retrieve the hmdb.org historical marker page for Tenney Park Lock and Dam (HTTP 403), so the marker's own inscription text is not included. Nominatim returned no result for a discrete "Schenk's Corners" node, "Willy Street Co-op East" as a named query, or "Vilas"/"Marquette" as neighborhood polygons — those were resolved via addresses and adjacent features instead. Wikipedia's Yahara River article does not document the locks, so lock history comes from Dane County Parks and Clean Lakes Alliance material surfaced in search.

area: Madison, Wisconsin — the Yahara Lakes isthmus and its greenspace ring (Dane County), spanning the UW–Madison Arboretum, Lake Wingra basin, Lake Mendota and Lake Monona shorelines, and the Cherokee Marsh headwaters
biomes: Restored tallgrass prairie (mesic, dry-mesic and wet-mesic; big bluestem, Indian grass, prairie dock, coneflower)
Bur-oak savanna (fire-dependent, open-grown 'wolf' oaks over grassland)
Dry oak woodland (white, black, bur, red oak on sandy/gravelly drumlin flanks)
Southern mesic hardwood forest (sugar maple, basswood, beech, ironwood — planted successional 'deep woods')
Boreal/conifer plantation (red and white pine, spruce, fir — the Leopold Pines and Boreal Forest)
Deep cattail marsh and open water marsh (Gardner, Redwing, Wingra, Castle/Warner marshes)
Sedge meadow and low prairie (Cherokee Marsh; one of the largest low prairies in the region)
Calcareous fen and shrub-carr (bog birch, willow, dogwood — Cherokee Marsh north)
Spring-fed seepage and springrun (Big Spring, White Clay Spring, Council Spring, Dancing Sands; 38+ springs historically fed Lake Wingra)
Shallow hardwater drainage lake (Lake Wingra: 1 sq mi, max 14 ft, ~120 days of ice)
Drumlin uplands and glacial ridge (Madison drumlin field, 5,000+ drumlins behind the Johnstown Moraine)
Urban lagoon, parkway and lock system (Tenney Park lagoons, Yahara River locks, Warner Lagoon, Vilas lagoons)
Effigy-mound ridgeline (Late Woodland panther/water-spirit, bird, bear, linear and conical earthworks)
Cultivated botanical collection and tropical glasshouse (Longenecker Gardens; Bolz Conservatory)
Reed canary grass monoculture / invaded wetland (a degraded 'blighted' biome in its own right)

landmarks.name: Curtis Prairie (UW–Madison Arboretum)
landmarks.character: 60 acres of tallgrass prairie, widely described as the world's oldest ecologically restored prairie. Planted from 1935–1941 by Civilian Conservation Corps crews under ecologist Ted Sperry, on land that had been a worn-out farm; renamed in 1962 for John Curtis, whose research here founded restoration ecology. Aldo Leopold's 1934 dedication called the Arboretum 'a reconstructed sample of old Wisconsin.' Big bluestem, Indian grass and prairie dock stand head-high by late summer; the whole system is maintained by prescribed fire, and stormwater from the city drains into it through Curtis Pond. The Arboretum is a National Historic Landmark for exactly this work.
landmarks.game_idea: The flagship Route. A grass ocean taller than the player sprite — the classic 'tall grass' mechanic taken literally, with sightlines dropping to zero and encounter rate spiking in the deep interior. Mow-lines and fire-breaks are the walkable paths, so the maze is made of what has been burned, not what has been built. Signature gimmick: a seasonal BURN CYCLE. A section of prairie that has been recently burned is black, open, low-encounter and safe to cross; unburned sections are impassable-dense. NPC 'restoration crew' trainers set fires on a timetable, so the traversable topology of the route physically changes between visits — a soft Rock Smash/Cut replacement that is ecological rather than brute-force. Fire-type and Grass-type encounters coexist here, and a Fire/Grass regional evolution should only trigger after the field has burned. Lore hook: this is the first place in the world anyone ever put a broken landscape back together, so it doubles as the tutorial ground for the game's whole restoration questline.

landmarks.name: Greene Prairie and the Grady Tract (UW–Madison Arboretum, south of the Beltline)
landmarks.character: A 47-acre prairie planted almost single-handedly by botanist Henry Greene between 1942 and the early 1960s — more than 130 species set by hand, each matched to soil and moisture, grading wet in the southwest to dry in the northeast; it now holds 220+ native species and is the most botanically exacting prairie in the region. It sits along the south edge of the Grady Tract, which also holds Southwest Grady Oak Savanna and Grady Dry Oak Woods, both fire-adapted. The prairie's southwest corner is being eaten by urban stormwater and a near-monotypic invasion of reed canary grass; fire and herbicide have not beaten it because the hydrology is broken.
landmarks.game_idea: A late-game 'gradient dungeon' where the encounter table is a literal moisture gradient — Water/Bug types in the boggy southwest, Ground/Rock and fire-adapted Grass types on the dry northeast knoll — so the player navigates by reading which plants are underfoot. The Grady Tract is cut off from the main Arboretum by a roaring highway (the Beltline), so reaching it needs an underpass tunnel: a short, dripping concrete cave segment as its own mini-dungeon gate. Antagonist mechanic: the reed canary grass invasion as a creeping BLIGHT ZONE — a spreading pale-green tile type that suppresses wild encounters to a single invasive Pokémon species and lowers the player's Grass-type stats. The player can't burn it out (fire has already failed); they must solve the water, i.e. fix the stormwater outfall upstream. Perfect structure for a multi-stage side quest whose reward is watching the blight tiles recede across several visits.

landmarks.name: Longenecker Horticultural Gardens (UW–Madison Arboretum)
landmarks.character: 35 acres of curated woody plant collections — one of the great lilac and crabapple collections in North America, plus viburnums and a large conifer collection — laid out in open lawn rows against the wild prairie next door. It is the deliberately artificial counterpoint to Curtis Prairie: rows, labels, and cultivars where everything else is remnant and restoration.
landmarks.game_idea: A tidy hub-garden 'town route' — safe, no wild encounters in the lawn, but a berry/apricorn farming and breeding site and the region's Move Tutor / Berry Master grounds. The crabapple and lilac rows bloom on a schedule, and a BLOOM WEEK event swaps in rare Bug and Fairy encounters that appear nowhere else. Because everything here is labelled and cultivated, make it the home of the region's Pokédex-completionist NPC and a 'cultivar' cosmetic-variant system: the same species in Longenecker shows up in ornamental color forms that don't occur in the wild areas, which the player can transplant back into restored ground. Visually it's the clean, sunlit breathing space between two much darker dungeons.

landmarks.name: Wingra Woods and the Big Spring (UW–Madison Arboretum)
landmarks.character: 52 acres of oak woods on the steep north-facing slope down to Lake Wingra — a true remnant, never plowed, only grazed. Sugar maple, basswood, beech and hemlock were planted in 1943–1964 and the stand is now converting to deep, shady sugar maple forest. The slope is pierced by springs: Big Spring is the largest in the watershed at roughly 320 to 670 gallons per minute, alongside West Spring and White Clay Spring; Council Spring and Dancing Sands lie just off Monroe Street. Effigy mound groups along McCaffrey Drive include panther and bird effigies with linear and conical mounds. The Ho-Chunk held that springs are the places through which animals enter the spirit world, and six Ho-Chunk villages once ringed the lake.
landmarks.game_idea: The best cave-substitute in the whole inventory, and it needs no cave. A dark, closed-canopy FOREST DUNGEON on a steep grade — descending switchbacks, permanent dim lighting requiring Flash or a lantern item, and a distinct 'deep woods' encounter table (Dark, Ghost, Bug, Poison) that replaces the oak-edge table once the maple canopy closes. The springs are the dungeon's set pieces: fixed, always-flowing water sources at the slope base that never freeze, so they are the one place on the map with Water encounters in the winter/ice state of the world. Build the spirit-world doorway idea straight in — a legendary or mythical water Pokémon that can only be met at a spring, at night, after the player has left an offering, with the encounter framed respectfully as a threshold rather than a capture. The effigy mounds along the ridge above are NOT dungeon loot: treat them as protected sacred ground, a no-dig zone that the villain team wants to excavate and the player stops them from touching. That inversion — a dungeon where the treasure is something you defend rather than take — is the strongest single design beat available in Madison.

landmarks.name: Gallistel Woods (UW–Madison Arboretum)
landmarks.character: 28 acres, a former oak savanna and an unplowed remnant, into which more than 1,000 sugar maple, red maple, basswood, beech and ironwood seedlings were planted between 1941 and 1961 — so it is a savanna being deliberately converted into a southern Wisconsin maple forest. A panther effigy and two linear mounds sit within it. It is denser and more enclosed than Wingra Woods and full of spring ephemerals.
landmarks.game_idea: The connective forest corridor between the prairie and the lake-slope woods — a short, atmospheric transition dungeon where the tree spacing visibly tightens as you walk north, so the player watches savanna become forest across a single screen-scroll. Good place for a 'two eras in one tile set' visual: ancient wide-crowned oaks left stranded inside a young maple understory, drawn as huge gnarled sprites that the maples are swallowing. Encounter design: overlapping savanna and forest tables where the savanna species are rarer each time you return, a quiet extinction the observant player notices. The panther effigy makes a natural shrine-clearing checkpoint with a healing spring or an ancient-move tutor.

landmarks.name: Lost City Forest (UW–Madison Arboretum)
landmarks.character: Mixed woodland grown over the ruins of Lake Forest, a failed 1911–1918 subdivision on the south shore of Lake Wingra. Promoter Chandler 'Bernie' Chapman planned an 800-acre suburb with its own gas, electric, water, schools and streetcars — on swampland. Too little fill was used; the roads literally sank and flooded. World War I and mismanaged money finished it. The UW bought the land in the 1930s. Concrete causeway remnants, buried sidewalks and sunken street grids still lie under the leaf litter and the marsh edge.
landmarks.game_idea: A ruined-city dungeon that is already written for you — Pokémon's recurring 'abandoned town swallowed by nature' with a real, verifiable history behind it. Design it as a submerged grid: fragments of a street plan visible as raised concrete strips through black water and cattails, with the walkable route following the one surviving causeway and forcing Surf detours where the road has gone under. Buried sidewalks appear as diggable tiles yielding period relics and fossils. Encounters: Ghost, Water, Poison and Steel (rusted infrastructure), with a rare 'urban ghost' line found nowhere else. The narrative reads perfectly as a cautionary tale the region's ecologists tell — build against the water and the water takes it back — which sets up the game's central conflict with a developer-flavored antagonist team.

landmarks.name: Teal Pond Wetlands and Gardner Marsh (UW–Madison Arboretum)
landmarks.character: Teal Pond is a sedge meadow and pond crossed by boardwalks; Gardner Marsh is open cattail marsh on the southeast side of Lake Wingra, adjoining Wingra Marsh (relatively undisturbed) and the Southeast and Redwing marshes. Together they form the Arboretum's wetland belt between the prairie uplands and the lake, a waterfowl and marsh-bird system.
landmarks.game_idea: A boardwalk route — a linear elevated path over water where the player physically cannot leave the planks, so encounters come to them from the reeds on both sides. Excellent for a controlled difficulty spike and for fishing/Surf gating: step off the boards and you need Surf, and the marsh floor is soft enough to sink into (a slow-tile mechanic that drains a step-timer). Cattail walls make natural sightline blocks for a hide-and-seek Bird trainer gauntlet. Dawn and dusk should swap the entire encounter table toward waterfowl and rails. A missing boardwalk plank is a great low-tech 'locked door' the player fixes with a fetch quest rather than an HM.

landmarks.name: Leopold Pines and Noe Woods (UW–Madison Arboretum)
landmarks.character: Leopold Pines is 21 acres of red and white pine with northern species, planted 1933–1937 in Aldo Leopold's era; a 14-acre Boreal Forest of spruce and fir sits nearby. Noe Woods is 41 acres of white and black oak woodland, named for the Bartlett-Noé family farm sold to the university in 1933. Together they are a deliberately transplanted piece of northern Wisconsin sitting in the south — a climatic island.
landmarks.game_idea: A cold-biome pocket dropped inside a temperate region, which is a genuinely useful map trick: a small dark conifer stand with needle-floor tiles, snow that lingers after it has melted everywhere else, and an Ice/Steel/Dark encounter table that otherwise belongs 300 km north. Justify it in-world exactly as reality does — someone planted it on purpose as an experiment — and let the player discover a research station NPC studying whether the transplanted species will survive a warming climate. Noe Woods next door is the sunny oak counterweight: an acorn-mast event where a bumper crop floods the woods with rodent and bird Pokémon, then a crash year empties it.

landmarks.name: Lake Wingra
landmarks.character: Madison's smallest lake: about 1 sq mi, average depth 9 ft, max 14 ft, 4 miles of shoreline, frozen roughly 120 days a year, draining via Wingra Creek to the Yahara River and eventually the Mississippi. The name is Ho-Chunk for 'duck'; the Ho-Chunk also called it the place where the turtle comes up. Historically fed by 38+ springs, its shore is almost entirely public — Arboretum on the south and west, Vilas Park, Wingra Boats and Edgewood College on the north. More than 230 effigy mounds ring it, the densest such concentration in North America. Stresses include mercury and PCBs, sedimentation, exotic species and nutrient loading; management includes carp removal.
landmarks.game_idea: The central Surf hub tying every Arboretum dungeon together — shallow, warm, weedy water, so the Water encounters skew to carp, turtle, duck and pike archetypes rather than deep-lake monsters. Two strong mechanics. First, ICE STATE: for a stretch of the calendar the lake freezes solid and becomes a walkable ice-puzzle field with sliding tiles and cracked-ice hazards, converting a Surf area into an Ice-type route and gating content by season. Second, the CARP PROBLEM: an overpopulated invasive fish Pokémon that clouds the water, suppresses every other encounter, and must be culled through a repeatable quest before rare natives return to the table — a legible, mechanical lesson in restoration that pays out in Pokédex entries. The lake's 230 mounds make its whole shoreline a ring of shrines, so treat Wingra as a sacred central body the region orbits, with a turtle-spirit legend surfacing from the water at the right time.

landmarks.name: Vilas Park and Henry Vilas Zoo
landmarks.character: In 1904 William F. and Anna M. Vilas donated a 63-acre tract on Lake Wingra's north shore in memory of their son Henry, on the binding condition that admission never be charged; the zoo opened in 1911 with a donation of five deer and remains one of only about ten free zoos in North America. Roughly 25 acres of high ground plus 35 acres built out of the bog, including four acres of lagoons. Above the zoo, on a ridge next to the lake, the Vilas Park Mound Group holds a bird effigy with an original wingspan over 200 feet, a linear mound and six conical mounds — with other mounds destroyed by development.
landmarks.game_idea: The region's 'city Pokémon facility' — a free, open, welcoming enclosure complex that reads as a Safari Zone crossed with a rehabilitation center. Because it is free by covenant, invert the Safari Zone: you pay nothing and you catch nothing; instead you observe, photograph, feed and befriend, and the reward is data, friendship stat and a rescued Pokémon that eventually chooses to join you. The lagoons make a small paddle-boat mini-route. The ridge above is a quiet, elevated mound shrine overlooking the water — a perfect contrast beat, five steps from a noisy family park into a 1,000-year-old bird effigy — and a natural site for a story revelation about the region's ancient people.

landmarks.name: Olbrich Botanical Gardens and the Royal Thai Pavilion
landmarks.character: Sixteen acres of outdoor gardens plus the 10,000 sq ft Bolz Conservatory, founded 1952 and named for Michael Olbrich, jointly run by Madison Parks and the Olbrich Botanical Society, on Lake Monona's east shore. The Bolz Conservatory is a glass pyramid 100 ft by 100 ft rising to 50 ft, holding 650+ plants across 80+ families and 475+ species and cultivars, with a waterfall, orchids and free-flying birds, held between 65 and 80 F. The Thai Pavilion — a teak sala 30 ft high, 40 ft long and 22 ft wide with gold leaf and the royal seal of the Thai Crown — was a gift from the Thai government and the Thai alumni chapter, opened in 2002; it is one of only a handful of salas outside Thailand. It is reached by a 155-ft arched bridge over Starkweather Creek and set in a tropicalesque garden.
landmarks.game_idea: Two set pieces in one location. The Bolz Conservatory is a TROPICAL BIOME DOME — an artificial glass dungeon with its own permanent weather (heavy humidity, sun-boosted Grass/Fire interactions), a waterfall climb, free-flying Flying-types indoors, and a small population of tropical Pokémon that exist nowhere else in the region and cannot survive outside the glass. Perfect for a puzzle where the player must not break the glass, and for a plot where the antagonists cut the heat and the player has 5 minutes to evacuate the tropical species before the Wisconsin winter kills them. The Thai Pavilion is the region's ceremonial arena: a gilded open-sided pavilion on an island, reached by a single arched bridge over a creek — a textbook duel platform, and a beautiful final-gym or elite-trainer stage where the bridge itself is the entry cutscene. Handle it with respect: it is a real royal gift and an active cultural site, so the sala should be honored ground, not a place things get smashed.

landmarks.name: Tenney Park and the Yahara River Locks
landmarks.character: 61 acres where Lake Mendota meets the Yahara River, given to the Madison Park and Pleasure Drive Association by lawyer Daniel K. Tenney in 1899 and built out 1899–1911. O.C. Simonds, a pioneer of the Prairie Style landscape aesthetic, designed a serpentine lagoon system dredged in 1901 to symbolize prairie rivers, with an island meadow standing for the prairie itself. The lock was originally built in 1847 as part of a flour mill; the city bought the site in 1896, built a boat lock and improved the dam. Now a City of Madison Landmark and on the National Register of Historic Places; the lagoons are a winter skating institution.
landmarks.game_idea: A canal-and-lock water route — the mechanical opposite of open Surf. Winding artificial channels with arched stone footbridges, an island in the middle, and an actual LOCK PUZZLE as the gate between the river level and the lake level: the player operates the lock to raise or lower the water, changing which channels are navigable and which lagoon floors are exposed for walking. That single mechanic gives a whole dungeon's worth of state-change puzzle without any new tileset. The serpentine 'symbolic prairie river' design is a lovely detail to surface in a plaque: a Victorian imitation of the wild rivers the region had already destroyed. In winter the lagoons freeze into an ice-skating rink route with a sliding-puzzle overlay and a seasonal festival.

landmarks.name: Warner Park
landmarks.character: Madison's largest urban park, roughly 180 acres at Northport Drive and Sherman Avenue, abutting Lake Mendota and enveloping a 28-acre lagoon dredged out of Castle Marsh in the late 1950s–early 1960s. The lagoon connects to Lake Mendota through a single 6-foot concrete pipe at its west edge, and a state–city agreement preserved enough wetland to support northern pike hatchlings. The park holds wetlands, woods, prairie and marsh islands, 141 recorded bird species, and deer, fox, muskrat, mink, beaver and otter. The advocacy group Wild Warner formed in the 2010s to defend the natural areas — a genuine fight between ballfields and habitat inside one park.
landmarks.game_idea: A split-personality route that is half stadium/festival ground and half genuine wild marsh, with the tension between them as the local story. The 6-foot concrete pipe linking lagoon to lake is a gift: a crawlable PIPE TUNNEL, the region's most literal cave — dark, echoing, one-tile-wide, full of Water and Poison types, and the migration corridor that fish Pokémon use to reach their spawning marsh. Build the local quest around it: something is blocking the pipe, the pike can't get through, the marsh nursery is failing. Marsh islands make excellent Surf-only micro-dungeons with one rare nesting Pokémon each. Beavers give you a dam-building puzzle that changes water levels; the 141 bird species justify the richest Flying-type encounter table in the region.

landmarks.name: Governor Nelson State Park
landmarks.character: A 422-acre day-use state park on the north shore of Lake Mendota in the town of Westport, near Waunakee, with over 8 miles of trails, sand beach and boat launch. Decades of prairie restoration have produced some of the finest restored prairie and savanna parcels in the area. Its southern section holds Late Woodland effigy mounds (circa 650–1200 AD) including the Wakanda Panther Effigy, a 358-foot panther mound, plus conical mounds, seen along the Woodland Trail.
landmarks.game_idea: The big open WILDERNESS ROUTE — the widest, windiest, least urban space in the inventory, and the natural 'you have left the city' threshold. Rolling restored prairie on a high shore with the whole lake laid out below: use long sightlines and a strong wind system that pushes the player, scatters seeds and affects Flying-type moves. The 358-foot panther mound is the single most usable ancient monument here: a colossal earthwork effigy of a long-tailed water spirit, visible in full only from a high point or from the air, which is a perfect late-game reveal when the player first gets a flying mount and looks down. Make it the seal or map-key to something rather than a dungeon to loot — the mounds are burial places, and the game should say so. The beach and boat launch give a clean transition point into the Lake Mendota water route.

landmarks.name: Owen Conservation Park
landmarks.character: About 97 acres on Madison's west side with 3.4 miles of dirt, grass and woodchip trail, once the summer retreat of UW French professor Edward T. Owen (1850–1931). With John Olin and Edward Hammersley, Owen donated land for a 12-mile pleasure drive and drove the creation of the Madison Park and Pleasure Drive Association, which bought and preserved parkland decades before the city grasped the idea. The park is now prairie restoration and oak savanna — coneflower, goldenrod and bluestem reclaiming old pasture — set high on a rise with long views over the city.
landmarks.game_idea: A hilltop OVERLOOK ROUTE that functions as the region's map-orientation moment: the player climbs out of the west-side neighborhoods onto an open savanna crest and sees the lakes, the isthmus and the capitol drumlin laid out, which is where you hand them the regional map. Widely spaced open-grown oaks make ideal savanna encounter design — clumped shade pockets with distinct tables between open grass. The vanished professor's retreat gives you a ruined foundation, an overgrown formal planting and a quiet mid-game NPC ghost story. Because Owen personally started the whole parks movement, make this the shrine of the region's conservation founders and the place a mentor NPC lives.

landmarks.name: Cherokee Marsh Conservation Park (North Unit) and Cherokee Marsh State Natural Area
landmarks.character: The largest remaining wetland in Dane County, sitting at the head of the Yahara lakes. The North Unit alone is roughly 947 acres with about 2.6 to 4.1 miles of dirt trail and metal/wood boardwalk, two observation platforms, two conical mounds and a carry-in canoe pier. Over 2,000 acres are protected in total across city, county, state and non-profit ownership, with 319 acres designated a State Natural Area since 1976, jointly owned by Madison and the Wisconsin DNR. The complex holds fen, shrub-carr (bog birch, willow, dogwood), sedge meadow, deep marsh and one of the largest low prairies in the region, with restored prairie, oak savanna and woodland on the uplands. Nesting sandhill cranes, bald eagle, osprey, Virginia rail, sora, sedge and marsh wren, swamp sparrow; American woodcock sky-dance in spring. It works as a living sponge, filtering runoff before it reaches the lakes.
landmarks.game_idea: The region's great WETLAND DUNGEON and the source of everything downstream. Design it as a vast, disorienting maze of head-high sedge and cattail where the only reliable navigation is the boardwalk network and the two observation towers — climb a tower to reveal a chunk of the map, exactly like a Ubisoft viewpoint but earned and thematically honest. Off-boardwalk travel means Surf, wading, or a mud-slow debuff, and shrub-carr thickets act as walls. This is where the mist/fog weather lives: reduced visibility, boosted Water and Fairy encounters, and the woodcock's spiraling display flight as a genuinely eerie ambient event at dusk. Give it a boss-scale sandhill crane Pokémon — a huge, red-crowned, bugling Flying/Ground guardian of the headwaters. Story spine: this marsh cleans the water for every other location in this inventory, so the villain plan to drain or fill it is an attack on the entire region's map at once, and the player fixing the marsh visibly improves water quality in Mendota, Monona and Wingra downstream.

landmarks.name: Turville Point Conservation Park
landmarks.character: About 64 acres of woodland on a point jutting into Lake Monona, a short walk from downtown, with 2.3 miles of trail. Large red, bur and white oak form the canopy over an understory that is being restored, plus a seven-acre prairie opening. Bought by Henry Turvill in 1854 and farmed by his family until 1967, when it was sold, reluctantly, to the city for the Monona Basin Project; designated a conservation park in 1998. Its undulating glacial topography is essentially unchanged since the ice left about 12,000 years ago.
landmarks.game_idea: A compact, dense OAK DUNGEON pressed right up against the skyline — the striking thing on the ground is that you are in deep dark woods with skyscrapers visible through the trunks, which is a fantastic composition for a route where the city is always in view but never reachable. Rolling drumlin topography gives you real verticality: ledges you can drop down but not climb, so the woods route is one-way in places and forces a loop. The seven-acre prairie opening is a bright clearing at the center — a natural boss arena or rest point, sunlit inside a dark dungeon. Nocturnal-heavy encounter table (owls, bats, Dark types) with the point itself as a migration stopover where the species list rotates by season.

landmarks.name: Olin Park
landmarks.character: About 47 acres on Lake Monona's south shore, named in 1923 for John M. Olin (1851–1924), who drove the 1910 public purchase of the site; formerly the Monona Lake Assembly grounds, then Monona Park. The 1884 pavilion survives as the locally landmarked Monona Lake Assembly Hall. It shares a continuous glacial drumlin landscape with adjoining Turville Point, with an unbroken skyline view across the water to the capitol.
landmarks.game_idea: The gateway town-plaza to the Turville woods dungeon: the Pokémon Center, mart, parking-lot NPC crowd and a historic pavilion that reads as an assembly hall — so make it the region's rally hall, where the local trainer league meets and where a chautauqua-style traveling show sets up. Best used as the point where the game frames its geography: stand on the shore, look across Lake Monona at the capitol sitting on a drumlin, and have an NPC explain that the whole city is built on the back of a glacier. That single conversation makes the drumlin motif legible for the rest of the game. Lakefront gives you the Monona Surf entry, fishing spots and a summer festival event.

landmarks.name: Edna Taylor Conservation Park
landmarks.character: A glacial drumlin rising above a broad ribbon of marsh forms the spine of this southeast Madison park, with about 1.3 miles of trail and a boardwalk, a spring, and oak stands. Edna E. Taylor sold 37 of her 98 acres to the city, combined with 10 city acres and 11 more bought from other owners. Six linear mounds and a panther effigy — the Pflaum-McWilliams Mound Group, on the National Register of Historic Places — run along the high drumlin on the eastern side. The adjoining Aldo Leopold Nature Center uses the park heavily for environmental education.
landmarks.game_idea: The clearest DRUMLIN-AND-MARSH cross-section in the inventory, and the best place to teach the region's geology as a level: a long whaleback ridge of high dry oak ground running between two arms of low wet marsh, so the route is a raised causeway with completely different encounter tables three tiles to the left and right of the path. High ground is Ground/Rock/Normal; low ground is Water/Bug/Poison; the boardwalk is the only safe crossing. The panther effigy and six linear mounds crowning the ridge make it the region's ancestral high place — put a Ruin Maniac-style archaeologist NPC here who is scrupulously respectful, in explicit contrast to the villain team's looters. With the Leopold Nature Center next door, this is the natural home of the game's environmental-education hub: a small ranger station that issues the restoration questline, tracks the player's habitat-recovery progress across every other site, and pays out for it.

notes:
STRUCTURAL READ FOR MAP DESIGN

Madison's greenspaces are not scattered — they are strung on one hydrological chain, which is the single most useful fact for a game map. Water enters the system at Cherokee Marsh (headwaters, largest wetland in the county), flows down the Yahara River through Lake Mendota (Governor Nelson, Warner Park, Tenney Park locks) across the isthmus and into Lake Monona (Olin, Turville, Olbrich via Starkweather Creek), while Lake Wingra sits in its own spring-fed side basin (Arboretum, Vilas) and drains in via Wingra Creek. That gives a natural route order: source marsh at the top, lakes in the middle, and a spring-fed sacred basin off to one side. Restoring the top of the chain visibly improving the bottom is a ready-made main-quest structure.

THREE MOTIFS THAT SHOULD RUN THROUGH EVERYTHING

1. FIRE AS A TRAVERSAL VERB. These prairies and savannas exist only because people burn them. A prescribed-burn cycle that opens and closes terrain is more interesting and more truthful than Cut, and Curtis Prairie, Greene Prairie, Owen and Governor Nelson all justify it.

2. GLACIAL BONES. Madison sits ~15 km inside the Johnstown Moraine of the Green Bay Lobe; the Madison drumlin field holds over 5,000 drumlins formed 20,000–15,000 years ago, and the State Capitol itself sits on one. Every 'hill' in this region is a whaleback ridge of glacial till running roughly northeast–southwest, with wetland in the troughs between. Build the entire heightmap on that grain and the map will feel coherent before you place a single asset. Edna Taylor and Turville/Olin show it most legibly.

3. EFFIGY MOUNDS AS PROTECTED, NOT PLUNDERED. Madison and its lakes had more than 1,500 effigy mounds — the state's mound-building capital — of which roughly 200 survive; Lake Wingra alone is ringed by 230+, the densest concentration in North America, and the world's largest bird effigy (624-ft wingspan) is on the Mendota Mental Health Institute grounds. These are burial places and remain sacred to the Ho-Chunk and other Indigenous nations. Strong recommendation: invert the franchise's usual 'ancient ruin = dungeon to raid' pattern. Mounds should be shrines the player defends from an excavating villain team, not tombs they crack open. That inversion is both more respectful and, dramatically, much fresher.

RANKING FOR THE THREE DUNGEON ARCHETYPES YOU ASKED ABOUT

Best CAVE substitutes (Madison has essentially no natural caves, so use enclosure instead of rock): Wingra Woods' dark closed-canopy slope with its spring mouths; the Warner Park 6-ft concrete lagoon-to-lake pipe (a literal crawlable tunnel); the Grady Tract Beltline underpass; the Bolz Conservatory as a sealed artificial biome.

Best FOREST dungeons: Wingra Woods (deep, dark, steep, spring-fed, mound-crowned) and Turville Point (dense oak with a skyline visible through the trunks). Gallistel Woods and Lost City Forest work as connective mid-length forests.

Best WILDERNESS/OPEN ROUTES: Curtis Prairie, Governor Nelson, Owen Conservation Park, Greene Prairie.

Best MARSH/WETLAND DUNGEONS: Cherokee Marsh North Unit (the flagship — towers, boardwalk maze, fog, crane guardian), Teal Pond/Gardner Marsh boardwalks, Warner Park's marsh islands.

Best RUIN dungeon: Lost City Forest, unquestionably — a real drowned 1911 street grid under a swamp forest, with buried sidewalks and a surviving causeway.

Best SET-PIECE ARENAS: the Royal Thai Pavilion on its island across a 155-ft arched bridge; the Monona Lake Assembly Hall pavilion (1884) at Olin; Governor Nelson's 358-ft Wakanda Panther Effigy ridge seen from the air.

TWO ANTAGONIST MECHANICS ALREADY WRITTEN BY REALITY

Reed canary grass at Greene Prairie: a spreading monoculture that flattens biodiversity and cannot be beaten by fire or chemicals because the underlying problem is broken hydrology. Model it as a blight tile-type the player must cure at the source, not at the symptom.
Invasive carp in Lake Wingra: an overabundant fish that clouds the water and suppresses everything else; a cull-and-recover loop that visibly restores the encounter table.

CAVEAT ON COORDINATES
All approx_lat/approx_lon values above were pulled from OpenStreetMap via the Nominatim geocoder against the named feature (all returned matching OSM feature types — grassland, forest, wetland, lake, park, nature_reserve, garden, zoo), and Lake Wingra's value is independently corroborated by Wikipedia (43.05361, -89.41972). They are centroids/representative points, not boundaries. Greene Prairie has no discrete OSM entry, so the coordinate given is the verified Grady Tract point it adjoins. No coordinate here was estimated or invented; Longenecker, Wingra Marsh (43.048646, -89.433574), Noe Woods (43.037115, -89.440460), the whole-marsh Cherokee centroid (43.154953, -89.382820) and Teal Pond (43.040858, -89.424312) were also verified and are noted here for map placement even where the landmark entry uses a paired feature's point.
