landmarks.name: Ushiku Daibutsu → Pokémon Tower, Lavender Town (Kanto)
landmarks.character: A 120 m bronze Buddha (100 m statue on a 10 m base and 10 m lotus platform) standing alone over flat Ibaraki farmland — visible for miles, single silhouette, one meaning: the dead. Bulbapedia gives it as the model for Lavender's tower; Lavender Town itself is placed at Ushiku / Narita, an area of Kofun-period burial sites.
landmarks.game_idea: Take the one structure in your area that is (a) taller than everything near it and (b) about death, memory or the past. Make it the town's only enterable tall building: 5–7 floors, no gym, no shop, wild encounters that are thematically wrong for the region, and a story gate on the top floor. The town around it gets no other landmark — a single-note town reads stronger than a mixed one.

landmarks.name: Mount Fuji → Mt. Silver (Kanto/Johto border)
landmarks.character: 3,776 m, straddling Shizuoka and Yamanashi, ~100 km south-west of Tokyo, in Fuji-Hakone-Izu National Park. The single most recognisable silhouette in Japan.
landmarks.game_idea: Reserve your area's highest point as post-game content, not critical path. Put it on the seam between two sub-regions so it doubles as a border, make it enterable only after the main story, and put the hardest single encounter at the top. The mountain's real job — 'the thing everyone can see and almost nobody climbs' — maps exactly onto an endgame gate.

landmarks.name: Yokohama + Yokosuka + Chiba → Vermilion City (Kanto)
landmarks.character: Bulbapedia calls Vermilion an explicit hybrid of three separate Tokyo Bay cities: Japan's largest seaport (Yokohama), a US naval base town (Yokosuka), and an industrial bay port (Chiba). The game also moves it to the wrong side of the bay.
landmarks.game_idea: The clearest single technique in the whole corpus: merge real settlements that share a VERB, not settlements that are near each other. Port + naval base + industrial dock = one town, one gym. Vermilion's American gym leader (Lt. Surge) and Electric type are Yokosuka's US base and Chiba's power infrastructure fused into a single gameplay statement. Do the merge before you do the map.

landmarks.name: Tōkaidō Shinkansen (Tokyo↔Osaka) → Magnet Train, Saffron ↔ Goldenrod (Johto)
landmarks.character: Bulbapedia identifies the Magnet Train as the Tōkaidō Shinkansen; in-game it is maglev, at 'over 340 mph', with an underground Saffron station. Construction on the real Chūō Shinkansen maglev on the same corridor began in 2015.
landmarks.game_idea: Model your inter-region express on the real rail line, then gate it TWICE: a broken-infrastructure quest (recover the stolen machine part from the Power Plant) and a ticket item (the Pass from the Copycat). One gate makes it a fetch quest; two gates make it feel like a national utility that had to be repaired and then authorised. Both stations are one room each — a rail terminus needs no more than a platform, a guard and a door.

landmarks.name: Tsūtenkaku, Osaka → Goldenrod Radio Tower (Johto)
landmarks.character: 108 m 1956 tower in the Shinsekai district, Naniwa-ku; observation deck at 91 m. Osaka's populist counterpart to Tokyo's towers.
landmarks.game_idea: Give the commercial/loud city a broadcast tower rather than a cathedral. Attach three functions to one building: a public utility (radio channels the player can tune), a collectible (the Radio Card), and a late-game villain occupation turning it into a vertical dungeon. Three uses of one silhouette is the cheapest content in the corpus.

landmarks.name: Kinkaku-ji, Kyoto → Bell Tower / Burned Tower, Ecruteak City (Johto)
landmarks.character: The Golden Pavilion, 12.5 m, top two storeys in gold leaf, three storeys each in a different architectural style, set over Mirror Pond. Notoriously, the real building was burned down by an arsonist in 1950 and rebuilt.
landmarks.game_idea: Where a real landmark has a destruction event in its history, build BOTH states and put them side by side: an intact sacred tower and its burned twin. You get a visual contrast, a two-dungeon town, and a legend hook (one bird per tower) out of a single historical fact. This is the highest-leverage move in the Johto map.

landmarks.name: Lake Biwa → Lake of Rage (Johto)
landmarks.character: Japan's largest freshwater lake, 670.3 km², entirely within Shiga Prefecture, supplying drinking water to ~15 million people in Kansai.
landmarks.game_idea: A 670 km² lake becomes a single circular water map roughly one screen across, ringed by a walkable shore path. Do not try to convey size; convey singularity — it is the only large still water in the region, so put the region's one anomalous event on it (the red Gyarados) and let the lake be a story location rather than a traversal one.

landmarks.name: Kōfuku-ji / Hōryū-ji, Nara → Sprout Tower, Violet City (Johto)
landmarks.character: Nara's temple pagodas — timber, multi-storey, with a central shinbashira pillar that sways in earthquakes rather than resisting them.
landmarks.game_idea: Sprout Tower's whole gimmick is that its central pillar sways — a real structural fact turned into a room description and an ambient animation. Pick one piece of genuine engineering trivia from your landmark and make it the room's visual verb. It costs one animation and buys the entire 'this was researched' feeling.

landmarks.name: Mount Aso caldera → Mt. Chimney + the ash routes (Hoenn)
landmarks.character: Caldera 25 km north–south by 18 km east–west; Takadake peak 1,592 m; an active crater reached in reality by a ropeway. Kyushu's volcanic centre.
landmarks.game_idea: Throw away the caldera (25 km will not fit) and keep three things: the crater rim as a walkable loop of ~30 steps, the ropeway as a literal cable-car transition, and the ash-fall as a unique route tileset with a collectible resource (volcanic ash → glassware). The correct compression of a volcano is not a smaller volcano; it is the crater, the lift, and the weather it causes.

landmarks.name: Hashima Island (Gunkanjima) → Abandoned Ship / Sea Mauville (Hoenn)
landmarks.character: 0.063 km² undersea coal-mining island off Nagasaki; four shafts to 1 km depth; peak population 5,259 in 1959; mine closed January 1974, island cleared 20 April 1974; reopened to visitors 2009.
landmarks.game_idea: The single best 'weird true fact' in the Japanese regions. An abandoned industrial hulk in open water becomes a mid-game dungeon reached by Surf and explored by Dive: flooded lower decks, scattered items, one key item that opens the rest. Keep the abandonment, drop the coal and the history entirely — the emptiness is the content.

landmarks.name: Tanegashima Space Center → Mossdeep Space Center (Hoenn)
landmarks.character: Japan's primary spaceport, on Tanegashima, the easternmost Ōsumi island ~25 miles south of Kyushu. Handles satellite assembly, launch vehicle testing, launching and tracking.
landmarks.game_idea: A remote island that is also a high-technology site is a gift: it justifies an out-of-place modern building, a two-floor interior dungeon, a villain-team raid, and a launch cutscene, all on a map you reach only by Surf. Put your region's one piece of advanced infrastructure on its most isolated island, not in its capital.

landmarks.name: Kikai caldera (submerged, north of Yakushima) + Santorini → Sootopolis City (Hoenn)
landmarks.character: A drowned volcanic caldera; the town's architecture is instead lifted from the white-and-blue Aegean. Geology from one place, buildings from another.
landmarks.game_idea: Split a landmark into FORM and MEANING and source them from different real places. Sootopolis takes its impossible geometry (a town inside a ring of rock, enterable only by Dive or Fly) from Japanese geology and its look from Greece. The result is unlike anything real and still reads as coherent. This is also the region's hardest gate, delivered by pure terrain rather than by an NPC.

landmarks.name: Ariake Sea / Kyushu's island fringe → Hoenn's southern archipelago and Route 105–134
landmarks.character: Kyushu rotated 90° counter-clockwise. Masuda stated the rotation was to increase playability and was related to the Game Boy Advance's horizontal screen. About half of Hoenn is water.
landmarks.game_idea: Rotate the source landmass to fit your display aspect ratio and your difficulty gradient — this is documented developer practice, not fan speculation. Then treat the sea as a legitimate biome with its own traversal verb (Surf on the surface, Dive below), rather than as a border. Water routes cost almost nothing to author and let you reuse one tileset for a quarter of the map.

landmarks.name: Ezo mountain chain (Hidaka, Ishikari, Kitami, Teshio, Yūbari) → Mt. Coronet (Sinnoh)
landmarks.character: Hokkaido's real spine of ranges, which splits the island climatically and historically. Sinnoh reproduces this as a literal wall dividing the region north/south.
landmarks.game_idea: The strongest structural idea in any Pokémon region. Convert your area's real mountain range into a hard wall with exactly three named crossings — a low tunnel early, a mid tunnel later, and a summit route at endgame. The range then does three jobs at once: it is the act structure, the climate boundary (snow only north of it), and the mythological centre. Terrain replaces level-gates.

landmarks.name: Kushiro-Shitsugen National Park → the Great Marsh, Pastoria City (Sinnoh)
landmarks.character: 268.61 km², Japan's largest reedbed, over 600 plant species; haven for red-crowned crane, huchen, Siberian salamander, specific dragonflies.
landmarks.game_idea: A protected nature reserve maps perfectly onto a Safari-Zone-style enclosure: pay an entry fee, get a step limit, no normal battles, unique species you cannot find elsewhere. The real-world conservation framing supplies the rules (a permit, a warden, a bounded area, a bird-watching platform) for free.

landmarks.name: Otaru canal and warehouse district → Canalave City (Sinnoh)
landmarks.character: Hokkaido port at 43.183 N, 141.000 E; canal lined with Victorian-style street lamps; preserved brick warehouses; the former Bank of Japan Otaru branch; was Hokkaido's financial centre before Sapporo overtook it.
landmarks.game_idea: A faded former capital is a better town than a current one — it gives you grand architecture with no crowds. Split the town in half with the canal and connect it with a drawbridge you can raise, so the town's own geometry is a puzzle. Put the region's library/lore building here because a declined financial centre is exactly where old records live.

landmarks.name: Abashiri → Veilstone City (Sinnoh)
landmarks.character: 44.017 N, 144.267 E. Meiji-era prison for political prisoners, now a museum, plus a working maximum-security prison. Sea of Okhotsk drift ice in winter; harbour ices over; least precipitation of any Japanese city; population fell 43,904 (1970) to 35,759 (2020).
landmarks.game_idea: A remote city defined by incarceration and isolation is where the villain team's headquarters goes. Reach it only through a mountain pass, give it a meteorite/monolith motif in place of the prison walls, and make it the one town where the buildings are hostile rather than helpful. The declining-population fact justifies a large map with few NPCs.

landmarks.name: Sapporo (grid plan + Odori Park + TV Tower) → Jubilife City (Sinnoh)
landmarks.character: 43.06194 N, 141.35444 E; ~1.96M people; laid out on an explicit grid of right-angled streets built around Odori Park, 'a green ribbon of recreational land bisecting the central area'.
landmarks.game_idea: When the real city has an unusual street plan, keep the PLAN and drop everything else. A rectilinear grid with a green strip through the middle is instantly legible at top-down scale and costs one tileset. Sapporo's TV Tower becomes the Jubilife TV building; the station becomes the Global Terminal. Two buildings plus a grid equals a two-million-person city.

landmarks.name: Furano / Biei / Hokuryū flower fields → Floaroma Town + Floaroma Meadow (Sinnoh)
landmarks.character: Hokkaido's famous banded seasonal flower fields — colour laid out in stripes across hillsides.
landmarks.game_idea: Some real places are pure texture with no structure. Do not give them a landmark; give them a TILESET and a resource. Floaroma is striped colour, a berry/honey economy, and nothing else — and it is one of the most memorable towns in the game precisely because it has no building worth entering.

landmarks.name: Brooklyn Bridge (+ Tokyo's Rainbow Bridge) → Skyarrow Bridge (Unova)
landmarks.character: 1,833.7 m total, 486.3 m main span, joining Manhattan's Civic Center to Dumbo/Brooklyn Heights across the East River. Sources note the Pokémon version blends it with Tokyo's Rainbow Bridge.
landmarks.game_idea: Bridges are the highest-value map type in the whole corpus: a long, thin, encounter-free corridor with a fixed camera and a view. They cost almost nothing, they read as spectacle, and because a real bridge is genuinely the only land link between two districts, a story gate placed on one never feels arbitrary. Build one per major water crossing and gate it with plot rather than an item.

landmarks.name: Grand Central Terminal → Gear Station, Nimbasa City (Unova)
landmarks.character: 40.7528 N, 73.9772 W. 44 platforms and 67 tracks, 41 in passenger service; third-busiest station in North America; ~67 million Metro-North passengers a year.
landmarks.game_idea: A monumental rail terminus becomes one concourse room with a departures board. Attach two systems to it: fast travel between towns, and an endgame battle facility riding the trains themselves (the Battle Subway). A station is the natural home for repeatable content because trains already imply 'do this again tomorrow'.

landmarks.name: Madison Square Garden → Big Stadium / Small Court, Nimbasa City (Unova)
landmarks.character: 40.75056 N, 73.99361 W. 19,812 for basketball, 22,000 for concerts; famously built directly on top of Pennsylvania Station.
landmarks.game_idea: MSG-on-top-of-Penn-Station is the model for stacking two verbs on one footprint. In your map, put the arena and the transit hub in the same town block so a single plaza serves both. Nimbasa fuses Midtown theatres, MSG and Coney Island into one town because they are all the verb 'entertainment' — merge by verb, again.

landmarks.name: Coney Island Wonder Wheel → Rondez-View Ferris Wheel, Nimbasa (Unova)
landmarks.character: 46 m (150 ft), at 3059 West 12th Street just north of the Riegelmann Boardwalk, Brooklyn.
landmarks.game_idea: A Ferris wheel is a rotating, enclosed, two-person space — i.e. a free cutscene stage with a built-in timer and no exit. Use your area's one amusement ride as the place where the plot delivers its private conversations. Almost no other map type gives you a locked room that the player enters voluntarily and enjoys.

landmarks.name: Williamsburg / Dumbo, Brooklyn → Nacrene City (Unova)
landmarks.character: Converted 100-year-old warehouses and lofts; Dumbo is literally an acronym for Down Under the Manhattan Bridge Overpass. Nacrene's gym is a museum inside a warehouse.
landmarks.game_idea: An adaptive-reuse neighbourhood gives you a gym that is also a museum inside a building that used to be something else — three layers of identity in one structure. Where your real area has industrial buildings repurposed for art, make the gym puzzle about the building's former function.

landmarks.name: Teterboro Airport, New Jersey → Mistralton City (Unova)
landmarks.character: A tiny municipality almost entirely occupied by an airfield — a real place where the airport is bigger than the town (populations of roughly 30 vs 70 in the comparison drawn).
landmarks.game_idea: Find the real settlement whose population is smaller than its infrastructure and make it your air hub. Seven houses and a runway is a complete town. Fly unlocks here, so the map's fast-travel system has a diegetic home in a place that is genuinely nothing but transport.

landmarks.name: Eiffel Tower → Prism Tower, Lumiose City (Kalos)
landmarks.character: 48.858222 N, 2.2945 E. 330 m to tip, 300 m architectural height. An iron lattice tower that is the single-image shorthand for an entire country.
landmarks.game_idea: Put the country's most famous silhouette at the exact geometric centre of the capital and make it the gym. Everything else in the city can then be generic, because the player orients by the tower from every street. One tower plus a radial street plan equals 'Paris' with no other Parisian content required.

landmarks.name: Place Charles de Gaulle / Étoile → Centrico Plaza and the Lumiose wheel (Kalos)
landmarks.character: 48.87389 N, 2.29472 E; 241 m across; twelve straight avenues radiating from one junction — the defining diagram of Haussmann's Paris.
landmarks.game_idea: Copy the DIAGRAM, reduce the count. Lumiose keeps the radial idea but drops twelve avenues to four (Vernal, Estival, Autumnal, Hibernal) plus five outer plazas in a pentagon, with North and South Boulevards as the rim and a canal between them. Five gates lead to five different routes. Because the layout streams street by street, the player never sees the whole city and therefore assumes it is larger than it is — occlusion is the cheapest way to fake urban scale.

landmarks.name: Mont-Saint-Michel (form) + Saint-Malo (site) → Tower of Mastery, Shalour City (Kalos)
landmarks.character: Mont-Saint-Michel: 48.636 N, 1.511 W; tidal island, ~7 ha, 92 m granite rock, tidal range about 14 m, historically reachable only at low tide — 'the incoming tide stranded, drove off, or drowned threats on foot'. Saint-Malo: 48.6494 N, 2.0261 W; walled granite city on a spit, with tidal islands (Grand Bé, Petit Bé, Fort National) reachable only at low tide.
landmarks.game_idea: The purest example of a real gate becoming a game gate. A causeway that is only passable at low tide IS a story flag — you do not have to invent a reason for the player to be turned away. Take any real access constraint (tide, avalanche season, opening hours, a ferry timetable) and use it verbatim as your progression lock. It is the one kind of gate players never resent.

landmarks.name: Palace of Versailles → Parfum Palace, Route 6 (Kalos)
landmarks.character: A ~300-year-old royal residence whose function was to display aristocratic power; formal gardens as a maze.
landmarks.game_idea: A palace is a garden puzzle with a building attached. Charge admission, make the hedge maze the actual content, and use the interior for a single collectible and a view. Aristocratic architecture is the cheapest way to signal 'this region has history' without writing any.

landmarks.name: Strasbourg astronomical clock → Anistar City sundial (Kalos)
landmarks.character: Strasbourg Cathedral's astronomical clock; Anistar is a psychic-themed city built around an enormous crystalline sundial.
landmarks.game_idea: Where a real city's icon is a TIMEPIECE, make the game's version literally time-dependent — the sundial glows at a specific hour and only then activates the Mega Ring. Real-world-clock mechanics are rare, memorable, and here they are motivated by the source landmark instead of being a gimmick.

landmarks.name: Le Havre → Coumarine City; Saint-Nazaire → Cyllage City; La Rochelle → Ambrette Town; Blois → Camphrier Town; Besançon → Snowbelle City; Amiens + Lille → Laverre City (Kalos)
landmarks.character: Kalos's second-tier towns map to real second-tier French cities, chosen for a single economic trait each: northern France's largest port, a shipbuilding town, a fossil/aquarium coast, a Loire château town, a cold Jura foothill city, and a merged pair of northern industrial cities.
landmarks.game_idea: Do not use only capitals. A region reads as a country when its minor towns are recognisably minor REAL towns with one industry each. Pick your area's port, its shipyard, its quarry, its château, its cold mountain town — one verb apiece — and let the capital be the only place with more than one idea.

landmarks.name: Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben) + the London Eye → Wyndon (Galar)
landmarks.character: Elizabeth Tower: 51.5007 N, 0.1245 W, 96 m. Galar's version pairs a clock tower with the 'Galar Hurricane' observation wheel. Galar's landmass is rotated 180° from Great Britain, so London becomes NORTHERN Wyndon.
landmarks.game_idea: Two silhouettes are enough for a nine-million-person city — a clock tower and a wheel — provided both sit on the skybox and are visible from the single boulevard you actually walk. Rotating the whole country 180° is the load-bearing move: it puts the capital at the far end of the difficulty ramp so the player's journey ends in the biggest stadium, which is the opposite of the real rail network but correct for pacing.

landmarks.name: Manchester Town Hall / Manchester and Liverpool → Motostoke (Galar)
landmarks.character: Manchester Town Hall: 53.47917 N, 2.24417 W; Alfred Waterhouse, High Victorian Gothic, inaugurated 1877. Motostoke is Galar's Industrial Revolution city, with railway motifs and steam architecture; its stadium quotes the Town Hall's neo-Gothic.
landmarks.game_idea: For an industrial city, put the civic Gothic building where the arena goes — the contrast between ornate municipal architecture and factory smoke IS the identity. Fire-type gym, brick and iron tileset, a rail viaduct running through the town, and terraced streets on a slope. Never give an industrial town a generic 'steampunk' read; anchor it on one dated, specific municipal building.

landmarks.name: Royal Crescent and the Roman baths, Bath → Circhester (Galar)
landmarks.character: Royal Crescent: 51.38694 N, 2.36833 W; built 1767–1774; 150 m long, 114 Ionic columns, the first crescent of terraced houses; uniform Palladian front with wildly varying rooflines behind, separated from the park by a ha-ha.
landmarks.game_idea: A curved terrace is a perfect game street: one repeated façade module, a single sweep, and a foreground/background separation you get for free. Add the hot spring at the centre as the town's shared social space, snow falling on Georgian stone for contrast, and TWO gyms (Ice and Rock) because a spa town legitimately has two natures. Note the real Crescent's trick — uniform front, chaotic back — as a direct instruction for façade authoring.

landmarks.name: Stonehenge (Amesbury) → Turffield's stone circle (Galar)
landmarks.character: 51.17889 N, 1.82611 W; outer sarsen circle about 30 m in diameter; two miles east of Amesbury.
landmarks.game_idea: A 30 m stone circle is already game-scale — one of the rare landmarks that needs NO compression at all. Drop it in at true size, put the gym mission inside it, and let the player walk the ring in about twenty steps. Search your area for anything under ~50 m across; those are free.

landmarks.name: Uffington White Horse (chalk geoglyph) → the Turffield hillside glyph (Galar)
landmarks.character: 51.5775 N, 1.56667 W; 110 m long; cut as deep trenches filled with crushed white chalk; dated by optical luminescence to 1380–550 BC; requires periodic volunteer 'scouring' or vegetation swallows it.
landmarks.game_idea: A hill figure is a lore delivery mechanism that needs no text: carve a Pokémon into the hillside and the player invents the myth themselves. The maintenance fact (it disappears without upkeep) is a ready-made sidequest. Look for the largest human-made GROUND drawing in your area — geoglyphs read beautifully from a tilted camera and terribly from ground level, so place the viewpoint deliberately.

landmarks.name: York walls + Edinburgh + Warwick Castle → Hammerlocke (Galar)
landmarks.character: Sources split between a York/Edinburgh walled-city read and a Birmingham/Warwick Castle read — i.e. the town is a composite of Britain's fortified silhouettes rather than any one city.
landmarks.game_idea: Your region needs exactly one WALLED town, placed at its geographic centre, containing the largest stadium and the energy plant. Walls give you a legible silhouette, a natural gate, and a reason the map narrows. Composite it from two or three real fortified cities so no one can say it is 'wrong'.

landmarks.name: Lake District + Peak District National Parks → the Wild Area (Galar)
landmarks.character: The Wild Area's southern half draws on the Lake District, its northern half on the Peak District's hills and valleys. It is Galar's single contiguous open space, weather-driven, with wild Pokémon far above the player's level near its edges.
landmarks.game_idea: The most important modern development in the whole corpus: replace hard walls with LEVEL GRADIENTS. A national park in the middle of the region gives you one large map that every town touches, with no fences — the player is repelled by a level-70 encounter rather than by a locked gate, so the world feels open while remaining sequenced. Author your one open area at the centre and let the linear towns hang off it.

landmarks.name: Isle of Man → Isle of Armor; Scotland → Crown Tundra (Galar)
landmarks.character: The Isle of Armor is explicitly the Isle of Man (a self-governing Crown dependency); the Crown Tundra is Scotland, isolated behind mountain ranges. Because Galar is rotated 180°, Scotland ends up in the SOUTH.
landmarks.game_idea: Reserve your area's offshore dependency and its remote highland for post-launch or post-game content. Both are already separated by real barriers (sea, mountains), so no artificial gate is needed — a train ticket and a story flag suffice. Their remoteness also justifies a different creature roster.

landmarks.name: Plaza Mayor, Madrid → Mesagoza's central square (Paldea)
landmarks.character: 40.415364 N, 3.707391 W; 129 m by 94 m; ten entrances and nine gates, each named (7 de Julio, Arco de Triunfo, Sal, Toledo, Cuchilleros…).
landmarks.game_idea: A 129 x 94 m arcaded square is close enough to game scale to use nearly unmodified — and its ten named archways are already the exits your map needs. Copy an enclosed plaza's footprint and gate list verbatim; it is one of the very few urban forms that survives compression intact.

landmarks.name: Sagrada Família → Naranja / Uva Academy, Mesagoza (Paldea)
landmarks.character: 41.40369 N, 2.17433 E; Gaudí; eighteen planned spires (Twelve Apostles, four Evangelists, the Virgin, and Christ), the central Christ tower at 172.5 m completed 20 February 2026, making it the world's tallest church.
landmarks.game_idea: Borrow a cathedral's ROOFLINE for a secular building. Paldea puts Barcelona's spires on a school in a city otherwise based on Madrid — the silhouette carries 'Spain' while the function carries the plot. Splitting a landmark's outline from its purpose lets you use the country's most famous shape without a religious building in your game.

landmarks.name: City of Arts and Sciences, Valencia → Levincia (Paldea)
landmarks.character: 39.45417 N, 0.35 W; Calatrava (and Candela for L'Oceanogràfic); L'Hemisfèric shaped as a giant eye, 110 x 55.5 m; the science museum as a whale skeleton; L'Umbracle 320 m of arches; L'Oceanogràfic 110,000 m² in a water-lily plan.
landmarks.game_idea: Where a real city has one architect's coherent modernist complex, make it a whole TOWN rather than one building — white shells, water, and glass everywhere, an electric-type gym, and a skyline visible from the coastal route. 'Levincia' is nearly an anagram of Valencia; the naming does half the recognition work.

landmarks.name: Roman Theatre of Mérida → Medali's open-air theatre (Paldea)
landmarks.character: 38.915389 N, 6.3385 W; built 16–15 BCE under Vipsanius Agrippa; grandstands about 86 m in diameter; capacity ~6,000. A UNESCO site.
landmarks.game_idea: An 86 m Roman theatre is another true-scale landmark: build it as-is and use the tiered seating as the gym arena. Roman ruins in an otherwise modern town are the cheapest way to state 'this country has 2,000 years of layers' — one structure, no exposition.

landmarks.name: Basque baserri farmhouses → Montenevera; Sagres, Portugal → Alfornada; Mérida/León → Medali; coastal Barcelona → Cascarrafa (Paldea)
landmarks.character: Paldea distributes regional Iberian vernacular around its map — Basque half-timbered farmhouses in the snowy north, Moorish-influenced architecture in the far south (Sagres), Roman in the west, Catalan fountains and plazas on the coast. Portuguese architectural and linguistic references cluster in the west, matching real Iberian geography.
landmarks.game_idea: Assign a different VERNACULAR BUILDING STYLE to each province and place them in their true relative positions. This is the single technique that makes an open-world country feel real: the player crosses an invisible line and the roofs change. It requires no landmarks at all — only three or four house meshes per province.

landmarks.name: Iberian culinary lexicon → every place name in Paldea
landmarks.character: Every settlement and geographic feature is named from food: meals, kitchen equipment, and cooking processes — Asado Desert, Glaseado Mountain, Socarrat Trail, Casseroya Lake, Porto Marinada, Cascarrafa, Los Platos, Mesagoza.
landmarks.game_idea: The cheapest and most consistent 'sense of place' device in the entire series. Pick ONE semantic field from the real culture (food, weather, textiles, mining terms, saints' names) and generate every toponym from it. It costs nothing, it survives translation, and it makes a hundred-name map feel authored by one hand.

landmarks.name: Route gates (the gatehouse building) — the load-bearing invention
landmarks.character: The small two-door building between every Kanto town and route. It is simultaneously a diegetic border checkpoint, a place to put a blocking NPC, and the engine's map-streaming seam. Saffron City's four gates are held shut by guards who simply want a drink.
landmarks.game_idea: Build one reusable gatehouse prefab and put it on every town/route boundary from day one. You then get, for free: a loading seam that nobody notices, a legal place to stand an NPC who says 'not yet', a shelter for a shopkeeper or a name-rater, and a visual full stop that tells the player they have changed zones. It is the highest return-on-effort asset in the whole design.

landmarks.name: Cycling Road (Route 17) — a motorway rendered as a route
landmarks.character: 10 blocks wide by 72 blocks tall in the Red/Blue data — 20 by 144 walkable steps, the longest map in Kanto. One-way downhill, banked with ledges you can only jump southward, requires the Bicycle to enter, and stands for the long run from Tokyo out to the tip of the Bōsō/Miura peninsula (~80 km).
landmarks.game_idea: Represent your area's one long expressway as a long, thin, one-way, item-gated corridor with directional ledges. Note the design lesson hidden in the numbers: Route 1 stands for ~49 km in 36 steps, Route 17 for ~80 km in 144 steps. Sixty percent more real distance got four times the tiles — because Route 17 is a set-piece and Route 1 is a tutorial. Tiles follow intended playtime, not kilometres.

notes:
HOW POKÉMON ADAPTS REAL GEOGRAPHY — a working brief. All game measurements below come from the pret/pokered disassembly (constants/map_constants.asm, `map_const NAME, WIDTH, HEIGHT` in 32x32px blocks; one block = 2x2 walkable steps; the Game Boy screen is 160x144px = 5 x 4.5 blocks). Real areas and coordinates are from Wikipedia. Ratios marked (calc) are my arithmetic from those two sources, assuming one walkable step ≈ 1 m of implied human scale; they are order-of-magnitude, not precise.

=====================================================
1. THE MEASURED COMPRESSION — AND WHY IT IS NOT A SINGLE RATIO
=====================================================
Verified Gen-1 map sizes (blocks, then walkable steps, then GB screens):
• Pallet Town 10x9 → 20x18 steps → 4 screens
• Viridian / Pewter / Cerulean / Vermilion / Fuchsia / Saffron 20x18 → 40x36 steps → 16 screens
• Celadon City 25x18 → 50x36 steps → 20 screens (largest Gen-1 city)
• Lavender Town / Cinnabar Island 10x9 → 4 screens
• Route 1 10x18 → 20x36 steps · Route 2 10x36 → 20x72 · Route 4 45x9 → 90x18 · Route 21 10x45 → 20x90 · Route 17 (Cycling Road) 10x72 → 20x144 steps, the longest map in the game

Real anchors: the Kantō region is 32,423.9 km² with a 2025 population of 43,509,179. Bulbapedia places Pallet Town at Shimoda (Izu peninsula tip) and Viridian at Mishima/Hakone — roughly 49 km apart. Cinnabar is Izu-Ōshima (~34.75°N) and Pewter is Maebashi (36.389°N) — about 182 km apart north-to-south.

Derived ratios (calc):
• Whole region, north–south: 182 km of real Japan across 306 walkable steps (Cinnabar 9 + Route 21 45 + Pallet 9 + Route 1 18 + Viridian 18 + Route 2 36 + Pewter 18 = 153 blocks) ≈ 600:1 linear, ≈ 360,000:1 by area.
• A single rural route: Route 1 = 36 steps for ~49 km ≈ 1,360:1 linear.
• Intercity link: Vermilion (Yokohama) to Saffron (Tokyo), ~28 km real, roughly 70 steps ≈ 400:1.
• Inside a city: central Tokyo, ~4-6 km across, becomes 40 steps ≈ 100–160:1.
• Settlement count: several hundred municipalities across Kantō's prefectures → 10 settlements.
• Population: 43.5 million → a few hundred NPCs. Bulbapedia lists Lumiose City, the second most populous city in the entire Pokémon world, at 416 residents, against Paris's ~2.1 million — about 5,000:1.

THE KEY FINDING: compression is deliberately NON-UNIFORM, by roughly an order of magnitude, and it is not even monotonic with real distance. Route 1 covers ~49 km in 36 steps; Route 17 covers ~80 km in 144 steps. Sixty percent more real distance received four times the tiles — because Route 17 is a bicycle set-piece and Route 1 is a tutorial. Cities are compressed the LEAST (~100:1) and empty countryside the MOST (~1,400:1), which is the inverse of what a cartographer would do and exactly right for a game.

The operative rule: THE MAP IS MEASURED IN SECONDS, NOT METRES. Budget each link by how long you want the player in it (a Gen-1 town crosses in ~10-15 s, a route in 30-90 s, the whole critical path in 15-20 hours), then distribute real geography over that budget. Where a real link is long and boring, do not lengthen the route — insert a CAVE, a BRIDGE or a GATE. Content, not tiles, is how the series expresses distance.

=====================================================
2. THE ABSTRACTION TECHNIQUES (six, in order of leverage)
=====================================================
(a) TOPOLOGY BEFORE GEOMETRY. Keep the adjacency graph and the compass relationships; discard true distances and coastline accuracy. Kanto preserves "capital in the middle, port to the south on a bay, mountains to the north-west, volcanic island offshore to the south" — and cheerfully moves Vermilion (Yokohama) to the wrong side of Tokyo Bay because the topology still reads.

(b) ROTATE AND FLIP TO FIT THE SCREEN AND THE DIFFICULTY RAMP. This is documented developer practice, not fan theory. Hoenn is Kyushu rotated 90° counter-clockwise; Masuda said the rotation was to increase playability and was related to the Game Boy Advance's horizontal screen. Galar is Great Britain rotated 180°, so London becomes northern Wyndon and the journey ends at the capital. Sinnoh is Hokkaido minus the Oshima Peninsula. Kalos snaps France's "hexagon" to a cleaner five-pointed star, and then reuses the pentagon as an iconographic motif on signage, clothing and the city plan. Unova abandons NYC's real shape for a rough loop so the game circuits.

(c) MERGE BY VERB, NOT BY PROXIMITY. This is the single most transferable technique. Vermilion City is a documented hybrid of Yokohama (port), Yokosuka (US naval base) and Chiba (industrial bay) — three cities fused because they share one function; the American gym leader and Electric type are the fused identity. Rustboro merges Fukuoka and Kitakyushu. Laverre merges Amiens and Lille. Motostoke merges Manchester and Liverpool. Nimbasa merges Midtown theatres, Madison Square Garden and Coney Island. Hammerlocke composites York, Edinburgh and Warwick Castle. Decide your 8-12 verbs first; then assign real places to them.

(d) SPLIT A LANDMARK INTO FORM AND MEANING AND SOURCE THEM SEPARATELY. Sootopolis takes its geology from the submerged Kikai caldera and its architecture from Santorini. Skyarrow Bridge is Brooklyn Bridge plus Tokyo's Rainbow Bridge. The Tower of Mastery has Mont-Saint-Michel's silhouette but sits at Saint-Malo. Paldea puts Barcelona's Sagrada Família roofline on a school in a Madrid-based city. The result is unlike anything real and still legible.

(e) DEMOTE WHAT WILL NOT FIT INTO TEXTURE. Anything famous but diffuse — a historic quarter, a cuisine, a street grid, a dialect — becomes a tileset, a music cue, an NPC line, or a NAME, never a building. Paldea's entire Spanish identity is carried more by its naming convention (every place named after food: Asado, Glaseado, Socarrat, Cascarrafa, Porto Marinada, Los Platos) than by any geometry.

(f) DELIBERATE INFIDELITY WHERE PLAY DEMANDS IT. Immediately north of Castelia City — i.e. north of "Lower Manhattan" — Unova places a vast desert, where reality has continuous metropolis. Players forgive it because the surrounding detail is dense and true. Budget yourself two or three of these per region, and put them where biome variety is thin.

Satoshi Tajiri on why the map is routes rather than continuous terrain (this is the original design charter): "We thought about how the real world we experience is made up local roads, highways, and lots of named roads that connect towns and cities… We figured 'well why not make a game like that?' And that's how we designed Kanto. This also had the advantage of making it so we didn't have to fill every inch of the map, the way we would've had to otherwise."

=====================================================
3. WHICH REAL LANDMARKS SURVIVE — THE FILTER
=====================================================
A landmark makes it into the game only if it passes all four tests:
1. SILHOUETTE — readable as one shape at sprite size, from more than a screen away. Ushiku Daibutsu (120 m, alone on flat farmland), the Eiffel Tower, Tsūtenkaku, Big Ben, Kinkaku-ji, a stone circle. A famous interior or a famous street fails.
2. ONE VERB — you can hand it exactly one gameplay function: a gym, a dungeon, a gate, a shop, a story beat. Pokémon Tower = the dead. Radio Tower = broadcast. Space Center = launch. Tower of Mastery = Mega Evolution. Anything you would have to explain in two sentences is cut.
3. UNIQUENESS IN REGION — it must be able to carry a town alone. Most Pokémon towns get exactly ONE signature structure. Two competing landmarks in one town is the commonest way an adaptation turns to mush. London is the deliberate exception at two (clock tower plus wheel) because it is the capital and the last stop.
4. TRUE ODDITY, IDEALLY. The best survivors carry one genuinely weird verified fact that can be rendered: Mont-Saint-Michel's ~14 m tidal range and drowned causeway; Hashima's undersea coal shafts to 1 km depth, abandoned in April 1974; Abashiri's Okhotsk drift ice and its Meiji political prison; the Uffington horse's chalk trenches that vanish without volunteer scouring; Mount Aso's ash-fall; the Royal Crescent's uniform front and chaotic rear. The oddity is the thing that makes an adaptation feel researched rather than sampled.

FREE LANDMARKS: anything under ~50 m across needs no compression at all. Stonehenge's sarsen circle is ~30 m; the Roman Theatre of Mérida is ~86 m across; Plaza Mayor is 129 x 94 m with ten named entrances that are already your map exits. Audit your real area for sub-50 m monuments and place them at TRUE SCALE — they are the only things in the whole map that will be honest, and players feel it.

=====================================================
4. HOW A REAL CITY BECOMES FOUR TO TWENTY SCREENS
=====================================================
THE TOWN TEMPLATE, unchanged since 1996 — this is the atomic unit of Pokémon urbanism:
  1 Pokémon Center (heal + save) · 1 Mart · 1 Gym or theme building · 1 signature landmark · 2-6 enterable houses at 1-2 NPCs each (each NPC = one line of worldbuilding OR one item) · N un-enterable façades to make up the mass · 2-4 exits, each into a NAMED route.
Everything a real city has that is not one of those slots goes into dialogue, tileset, or the town's name.

THE FAÇADE RATIO. Celadon City is the largest Gen-1 city at 25x18 blocks (~20 screens) yet has only about a dozen enterable doors — Department Store, Game Corner, restaurant, hotel, condominium, gym, Center, Mart, hideout stairs. The building mass exists purely to be walked around. Working budget: roughly ONE ENTERABLE DOOR PER TWO TO THREE SCREENS of city. This is what lets 40 steps read as "a metropolis" rather than "a village with tall houses".

DENSITY TRICKS BY GENERATION — each solves the same problem differently, and all four are still usable:
• Gen 1-3 (Saffron, Celadon): flat and wide. Density comes from CLUSTERING the few real doors and building a regular grid of identical façades around them. Silph Co., an eleven-floor tower, IS the whole corporate district compressed into one dungeon.
• Gen 5 (Castelia): the CITY AS CANYON. Four streets total, walled by un-enterable skyscrapers, camera tilted up. Manhattan's density is conveyed by OCCLUSION rather than footprint — you cannot see out, so you assume it continues.
• Gen 6 (Lumiose): RADIAL PLAN PLUS STREAMING. A wheel of North and South Boulevards split by a canal, four seasonal avenues as spokes, Prism Tower at Centrico Plaza in the centre, five outer plazas in a pentagon, and five gates to five routes. You never see the whole city at once, so it feels far larger than it is. Compare Place Charles de Gaulle: twelve real avenues at 241 m across, reduced to four.
• Gen 8-9 (Wyndon, Motostoke, Mesagoza): TERRACED SLOPE PLUS PAINTED SKYBOX. Build one processional street up a hill, put the rest of the city in the background art. Mesagoza is a stepped hill town with a single grand stair up to the academy, and because the surrounding country is real navigable terrain, the city's smallness is contextualised rather than exposed.

WORKED BEFORE/AFTER — TOKYO → SAFFRON CITY.
Before: Chiyoda and Shinjuku wards, roughly 30 km² combined, over a million daytime workers, Tokyo Station, the Marunouchi office district, Shinjuku's nightlife.
After: 20x18 blocks — 40x36 walkable steps, 16 Game Boy screens, crossable in a few seconds. A regular grid of identical office façades; about six enterable doors; ONE eleven-floor tower (Silph Co.) standing in for the entire corporate economy and doubling as the game's mid-point villain dungeon; a Psychic gym; and four gatehouses on the compass points, all four closed by guards who want a drink. Nightlife and shopping were split off into a SEPARATE town (Celadon = Shinjuku) because they are a different verb. Compression ≈ 120:1 linear (calc).

WORKED BEFORE/AFTER — 49 km OF THE IZU PENINSULA → ROUTE 1.
Before: Shimoda to Mishima, ~49 km of Route 414 through the Amagi mountains, hot-spring towns, hairpins, a tunnel.
After: 10x18 blocks = 20x36 steps. Two ledges, one strip of tall grass, Pidgey and Rattata, and an NPC who hands you a Potion. No trainers. Everything the real road contains was deleted because this segment's job is to teach three verbs (walk, encounter, ledge). ~1,360:1 (calc).

=====================================================
5. REAL TRANSPORT LINKS → ROUTES AND GATED PASSAGES
=====================================================
TRANSLATION TABLE (real feature → in-game device):
• River / estuary / bay → water route requiring Surf, or a bridge map
• Bridge → a long thin ENCOUNTER-FREE corridor with a fixed scenic camera; the natural home for a story gate (Skyarrow = Brooklyn Bridge, 1,833 m, the genuine sole land link between two districts)
• Mountain range → either a cave dungeon requiring Flash (Mt. Moon, Rock Tunnel, Chargestone) or a hard WALL with 2-3 named crossings (Mt. Coronet = the Ezo chain: a low tunnel early, a mid tunnel later, the summit at endgame)
• Road / rail tunnel → Diglett's Cave, the Underground Path, Galar Mine
• Motorway or toll road → Cycling Road: long, thin, one-way, banked with directional ledges, requires the Bicycle
• Ferry → S.S. Anne, Seagallop, ticket-gated
• Shinkansen → the Magnet Train, Goldenrod↔Saffron (= Osaka↔Tokyo), double-gated by a repair quest AND a pass
• Metro → Gear Station and the Battle Subway; Grand Central's 67 tracks become one concourse plus endgame content
• Airport → Mistralton City (Teterboro, NJ — a real municipality smaller than its airfield); unlocks Fly
• Border checkpoint → the ROUTE GATE building: diegetic checkpoint, NPC anchor, and engine streaming seam in one prefab
• Toll / permit → Safari Zone or Great Marsh: entry fee, step limit, no ordinary battles, exclusive species (directly modelled on Kushiro-Shitsugen's 268 km² protected wetland)
• Tide / seasonal closure → a scripted story gate (Mont-Saint-Michel → Tower of Mastery)
• Private land / civic obstruction → the Snorlax, the Cut tree, the officer, the thirsty guard

THE SIX GATE TYPES, and when each is appropriate:
1. TRAVERSAL/ABILITY gates — Cut, Surf, Strength, Flash, Rock Smash, Waterfall, Dive, Rock Climb, the Bicycle, Rotom Bike modes, Koraidon/Miraidon's climb-swim-glide. Best for permanent terrain classes.
2. ITEM gates — Poké Flute, S.S. Ticket, Magnet Train Pass, Bike Voucher. Best for one-off links.
3. BADGE gates — badges license the HMs; the Route 22 guard checks a badge. Best for enforcing global order.
4. NPC/SOCIAL gates — the Saffron guards who want a drink; a Snorlax asleep in the road; grunts on the Underground Path. Best for temporary, comic, low-stakes blocking.
5. STORY-FLAG gates — bridges, causeways, the Space Center. Best where the real world already has a gate.
6. SOFT gates — Galar's Wild Area and Paldea's open world. Nothing blocks you; a level-70 wild Pokémon does. Best for open-world maps.

THE MODERN SHIFT, and the most important thing to copy: Galar and Paldea moved gating OFF horizontal walls and ONTO level gradients and vertical traversal upgrades. Paldea's map is fully open from the start; its three questlines each impose their own internal order, and the ride Pokémon's climb/swim/glide unlocks re-gate the terrain VERTICALLY. The player is never told no; they are told "not with these legs."

THE GOLDEN RULE OF GATE PLACEMENT: put your gates where the real world already has one — a bridge, a tunnel mouth, a tide, a ferry, a toll, a border, a mountain pass, a park gate. A gate on a bridge is invisible. A gate in an open field is a wall, and players resent it.

=====================================================
6. RECOGNISABLE VERSUS GENERIC — THE STACK
=====================================================
In descending order of how much recognition each layer buys per unit of work:
1. NAMING REGISTER. The cheapest device in the corpus. Paldea generates every toponym from one semantic field (food). Galar uses genuine English place-name morphology (-wick, -hurst, -stoke, -chester: Postwick, Wedgehurst, Motostoke, Circhester; Stow-on-Side puns on Stow-on-the-Wold). Kalos uses French cognates (Coumarine, Camphrier, Anistar, Cyllage). Numbered routes plus locally-registered town names deliver "country" before a single tile is drawn.
2. ONE UNMISTAKABLE SILHOUETTE PER TOWN, visible on approach.
3. THE LOCAL ECONOMIC VERB, expressed in props: cranes and a hull at the port, a pit-head and coal carts at the mine, steam and Georgian stone at the spa, a viaduct and brick at the mill town. This is what makes Motostoke read as Manchester rather than as Generic Steampunk Town.
4. VERNACULAR BUILDING STOCK VARIED BY PROVINCE. Paldea's single strongest move: Basque baserri farmhouses in the snowy north, Moorish-influenced forms in the far south, Roman in the west, Catalan plazas and fountains on the coast, Portuguese references clustered west — all in their true relative positions. The player crosses an invisible line and the ROOFS CHANGE. Three or four house meshes per province and you are done.
5. ONE TRUE WEIRD FACT PER REGION, rendered faithfully.
6. A CULTURAL CONTRAST AXIS as the region's spine. Kanto (modern, technological) versus Johto (traditional, temples) mirrors the genuine Kantō/Kansai opposition; Sinnoh's mountain splits the region into two climates; Galar splits rural south from industrial north.
7. MUSIC AND AMBIENCE keyed to region.

WHAT MAKES AN ADAPTATION GO GENERIC: a landmark with no gameplay verb; two competing silhouettes in one town; honouring real distances (this is the commonest failure — proportional maps are boring maps); routes of uniform length; using the national FLAG COLOURS instead of the national BUILDING MATERIALS; and picking only capitals. A region reads as a country because its second-tier towns are recognisably real second-tier towns with one industry each — Le Havre, Saint-Nazaire, La Rochelle, Blois, Besançon.

=====================================================
7. A TRANSFERABLE RECIPE
=====================================================
1. Draw the real area's ADJACENCY GRAPH: settlements as nodes, real transport links as edges. Discard everything else.
2. Cull to 8-12 nodes. Merge any nodes that share a verb.
3. Give each node exactly ONE verb and ONE silhouette. Reject landmarks failing the four-part filter in §3.
4. Rotate or flip the whole graph so the difficulty ramp runs the long axis and the capital lands at the far end.
5. Convert each edge to a route type by its REAL obstacle (water→Surf or bridge; mountain→cave; tunnel→tunnel; rail→fast travel; motorway→bike road).
6. Place gates only on edges that already have a real-world gate.
7. Budget tiles by intended seconds of play, not by kilometres. Expect a 10x spread between your most and least compressed links, with cities compressed LEAST.
8. Give each town one landmark, four to eight enterable doors, and façade for the rest.
9. Generate all names from one local semantic field.
10. Keep one verified weird fact per area and render it exactly. Then allow yourself two or three deliberate lies where the biome variety is thin.
